Mini-lesson on retired or overused verbs
How do I help students stop using got, put, make, do in their writing?

How do I teach students to kill vague verbs like 'get' or 'put'?

How do I teach 8th graders to replace tired verbs with precise action verbs?
entries.complete_ml_text:
Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 11: Teaching Word Choice, Mini-Lesson #3: Eliminate dead/retired verbs

Some words are weak because they are overused. Others may be weak because they are vague. But some words are both — overused and vague! When those words are verbs, they should be eliminated. If the verb is the engine to the sentence, then it must be powerful and precise.

Identify the most overused and vague verbs that students tend to use (e.g., get/got, go/went, did/do, make/made, take/took, put, etc.).

The reason these verbs are so weak is that each of them constitutes so many different possibilities. How did you "get" it? Steal it, sneak it, snatch it, grab it, purchase it, contract it? The context of the sentence will determine the most appropriate "get" verb. It's more than just replacing the verb with a set of choices. Writers have to reread the piece and determine which verb most precisely captures the action.

Reveal the Get Outta Here handout. As a class, brainstorm synonyms for "get" that would fit the context of each sentence. (For an extra challenge, avoid repeating any verbs.)

Spend a few minutes having students flip through their own previous writings to assess how often they see this dead/retired verb in their own pieces.

Conclude the lesson by building a wall chart that will list the dead or retired verbs. Write get/got on the chart.

The R.I.P. tombstone or a retired jersey number represent the forever nature of "dead" verbs.

Independent Writing: Identify additional verbs students need to bury/retire (e.g., take/took, make/made, put, go/went, did/do, etc.). Pairs use the short passages to identify more precise verbs. Then bury/retire the original ones by adding them to the wall chart. Eventually, students revise previous pieces replacing the dead/retired verbs with stronger ones.

hyde_summaries: How do I teach students to minimize helping and linking verbs?
Mini-lesson on reducing 'to be' and 'to have' verbs
How do I help students eliminate is, are, was, has from sentences?
Lesson on strong action verbs over linking verbs
How do I teach students to revise to active verbs?
Minimize-helping-verbs mini-lesson
How do I teach students to replace forms of 'to be' with active verbs?
entries.complete_ml_text:
Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 11: Teaching Word Choice, Mini-Lesson #4: Minimize helping and linking verbs

When emphasizing action verbs, simultaneously limit the number of linking and helping verbs students utilize.

Reveal a writing sample that includes strong word choice, but weak verb choice (e.g., "Autumn"). Identify the precise words that are powerful (e.g., giddy children, brittle leaves, earthy aroma, gooey perfection, crimson leaves, etc.). Point out that these are adjectives and nouns. Then, list the weak verb choices (e.g., have, goes, is, etc.).

Identify these as helping and linking verbs and mark every one with a heavy black X. Count how many Xs are on the page.

Model how to revise the sentences to eliminate or replace the helping/linking verbs with strong action verbs. This may include:
- Substituting the helping verb/verb with a single action verb (e.g., are baking → bake).
- Restructuring the sentence to eliminate the linking verb, adding in a new powerful action verb (e.g., Trees are sad. → Trees shiver and sigh.).
- Adding descriptive detail to the sentence (e.g., The moon is behind a cloud. → The moon peeps out behind a cloud.).
- Replacing a weak phrase for a single, stronger action verb (e.g., The moon is high above... → The moon governs...).

Conclude the lesson with an additional key instructional point: A piece with only action verbs is not necessarily the goal. Too much information all the time creates very dense sentences. It's common for a writer to include an occasional linking verb to provide some relief for the reader.

Independent Writing: Students select a previous draft and mark each helping and linking verb with an X. Announce how many helping/linking verbs can be in their revision (e.g., You can use up to three helping and/or linking verbs. All others must be substituted, replaced, or revised.).

Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 11: Teaching Word Choice, Mini-Lesson #5: Weave in close-up details

An author uses his word choice to create a reader's visualization. In order to achieve this, the writer must provide powerful and precise close-up details.

Project two similar images (e.g., two monsters). Be sure the images are more similar than they are different. Then read a short description about one of the images, asking students to identify which image the passage is referencing.

After students select the "answer" image, discuss the details that were most helpful in their decision-making (e.g., flawless skin, teeth of varying lengths, etc.). Note that without those close-up details, they would not have known which image was correct.

Explain that had the author used vague description (e.g., a scary monster, gross teeth, black eyebrows, gloved hands, etc.), students would not have known which image was being referenced. This is the kind of precision and close-up details students need to include within their writing.

Model how to craft a close-up-detail description:
- Reveal another set of similar images (e.g., two vases of flowers). If students are ready for more of a challenge, provide them three similar-looking images.
- Identify which of the images will be "the answer" (e.g., Image #2).
- Create a list of general descriptive phrases that is true for both/all of the images.
- Study the images more carefully. Look for something that makes Image #2 different than the other(s). List the details unique to the "answer" image only.
- Weave together a short description that includes details relevant to both/all images and those precise ones applicable to only "the answer."

Independent Writing: Students play Guess the Image. Provide students with two similar photographs. Students secretly select one to be the "answer" and list details relevant to both scenes in the left column. Then, they focus on what makes the "answer" image unique, listing those close-up details in the second column. Students generate a quick write to read aloud to their peers.

entries.complete_ml_text:
Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 12: Teaching Sentence Fluency, Mini-Lesson #1: Assess sentence-length variety

One characteristic of strong sentence fluency is varied sentence length. When sentences are similar in length, the piece has a numbing sameness. Strong writing includes an occasional short or long sentence amid the medium-length ones. Define a short sentence as being 1-5 words and a long sentence as being more than 10 words. Everything else is considered medium.

With an understanding of what constitutes short, medium, and long sentences, assess the sentence-length variety of an anchor paper:
- Read the piece aloud, applying punctuation as indicated by the author. (Students might move their arms or stretch Slinkies per sentence while the teacher reads aloud.)
- Note that the piece is grammatically and mechanically correct. However, the overall sound of the writing is nothing special; it has a numbing sameness to it.
- Count up the number of words per sentence, noting them within the Charting Fluency handout.
- Label each sentence small (S), medium (M), or large (L) in the third column.

Read the revised writing, applying punctuation as indicated by the author:
- Note the number of words per sentence and the S, M, or L label on the Charting Fluency handout.
- Compare the overall sound and charted sentence-length variety of the original piece to that of the revision. How is the mood different between the two versions?
- Acknowledge that medium-length sentences are necessary in order to appreciate the drama of the other two lengths.

Clarify that a piece can be conventionally correct and still weak in sentence fluency. This trait is about the sound of the writing — not the look of it.

Illustrate sentence length with a Slinky. Good writing makes the Slinky move; it passes the Slinky Test. Have students adjust the Slinky after every sentence to demonstrate its length: Compress the Slinky for a short sentence (1-5 words). Adjust the Slinky to represent "medium" sentences (6-10 words). Stretch the Slinky for a long sentence (more than 10 words).

Independent Writing: Assess the sentence-length variety of multiple short pieces previously written (or single paragraphs from a longer piece). Provide a separate Charting Fluency handout per writing. Students are not revising; they are only assessing.

Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 12: Teaching Sentence Fluency, Mini-Lesson #5: Create long and efficient sentences

As students attempt to create longer sentences, they often add words but not information. Teach the difference.

Although long sentences include more words, there should be no filler or fluff. Every word counts. Long sentences are not just short sentences stretched out with more words. Longer sentences must include more information. That's the notion of efficient writing.

Reveal examples depicting long and inefficient versus long and efficient:

ORIGINAL: He got a broom.
LONG & INEFFICIENT: He went over and got a broom that he could then use.
LONG & EFFICIENT: He ran over, dug through a pile, and found a broom.

ORIGINAL: It rained a lot yesterday.
LONG & INEFFICIENT: It was very wet and really rainy all day long and all night long yesterday.
LONG & EFFICIENT: Yesterday it misted most of the morning, drizzled on and off in the afternoon, and thunder-stormed throughout the night.

If something is efficient, then it maximizes productivity with the least amount of effort. Therefore, efficient writing maximizes the information using the fewest words.

Reveal 7 Strategies to Lengthen Sentences. Then, identify which strategies were used in the two examples above. Note that it's possible to utilize more than one strategy in each sentence.

Independent Writing: Provide a list of short sentences and long/inefficient counterparts. Students stretch each one, applying various techniques from the 7 Strategies to Lengthen Sentences handout.

Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 12: Teaching Sentence Fluency, Mini-Lesson #6: Add rhythm with parallel structure

Parallelism — writing in word patterns — is a major contributor to strong sentence fluency. Introduce this technique using baby snap-beads. Three red beads snapped together represents a noun, noun, noun pattern. A blue-red pattern of beads represents an adjective-noun, adjective-noun, adjective-noun pattern.

Explain that items in a series should be presented in the same pattern, meaning each item between the commas should utilize the same part(s) of speech. Then reveal a non-parallel sentence and characterize it with colored beads that do not create a pattern. Emphasize that although a sentence can be mechanically correct, it doesn't sound fluent or smooth. There is no rhythm to it.

To create parallelism with items in a series, the writer first selects one structure from those in the list and then revises all the others to create the same word pattern.

Reiterate that there is no correct pattern. In fact, return to the same original sentence and revise it again using a different structure.

ORIGINAL: At the grocery, we bought green grapes, a bunch of bananas, and apples.
REVISION: At the grocery, we bought green grapes, yellow bananas, and red apples.
SECOND REVISION: At the grocery, we bought a container of grapes, a bunch of bananas, and a bag of apples.

ORIGINAL: After ball practice, I'm going to eat something, take a long hot shower, and sleep.
REVISION: After ball practice, I'm going to eat, sleep, and shower.
SECOND REVISION: After ball practice, I'm going to eat a big filling meal, take a long hot shower, and sleep for several uninterrupted hours.

Independent Writing: Students reread previous drafts, identifying sentences that are nonparallel. They rewrite each one, creating two different parallel structures using the Experiment with Parallelism template.

Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 13: Teaching Conventions, Mini-Lesson #1: Reread to hear punctuation

For students to apply punctuation marks accurately within their own writing, they need to know more than just the rules. They need to know how the different marks affect the reader's voice.

Reveal the Hearing Punctuation chart. More than the rule behind each mark, identify its impact on a reader's fluency. (Start with only the three end marks and the comma. Slowly reveal additional punctuation on the chart later in this lesson or in follow-up lessons.)

When self-editing and whisper-reading, a writer should listen to himself. When his voice stops at the end of a complete thought, he should confirm he placed a period there. If he pauses in a sentence, then he should check for a comma. If writers want readers' voices to stop, pause, get loud, or go up, then the writer has to indicate that with the appropriate punctuation.

Model how this looks and sounds. Project an excerpt of text and read it aloud, emphasizing the period stops, comma pauses, volume changes, etc. Each time, reference that the voice change is because of a punctuation mark.

Reveal a previous draft. The teacher will read it aloud the way it was meant to sound. Confirm that each sentence has the marks to match the read-aloud voice. (NOTE: Choose a draft that has some missing or inaccurate punctuation in order to model the editing process, too.)

Students who read right through punctuation marks, never stopping, pausing, or taking a breath, tend to omit punctuation within their own writing. Consequently, this lesson improves their application of writing conventions and their reading fluency.

Independent Writing: Using previous drafts, students will self-edit for punctuation using the Read Up, Write Down strategy.

Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 13: Teaching Conventions, Mini-Lesson #2: Introduce a Speaking Punctuation procedure

Writers choose punctuation when drafting a piece in order to communicate the intended message. "I love spring!" is different from "I LOVE spring!" and "I love spring?" Each of those sentences produces a different message.

Consequently, punctuation needs to become a focus during the composing step of the writing process — not just the editing stage.

To highlight punctuation within a first draft, introduce a new class procedure — Speaking Punctuation.

Explain that for short stints of time, students will engage in conversations with peers, and when they do, they will have to insert the appropriate punctuation as if they were writing down the conversation. For example, if explaining a weekend activity, the teacher might say, "I went to my uncle's (apostrophe s) house and helped plant trees, (comma) bushes, (comma) and flowers (period)."

It seems a little awkward at first, but it doesn't take long for students to get the hang of it.

Model a second example: "After we play (capital S) Speaking (capital P) Punctuation, (comma) we will read silently within our library books (period)."

The benefit to this activity is that the students are thinking about their punctuation marks when talking, which translates into them thinking about their punctuation marks during first-draft writing, too.

Independent Writing: Pairs practice Speaking Punctuation while the teacher eavesdrops on conversations.

Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 13: Teaching Conventions, Mini-Lesson #3: Indent for new information

Students need to know when to indent or start a new paragraph. It's not about counting the number of sentences.

An indent serves an important purpose for the reader. It's a visual indication that there is a shift in information. It does not matter how many sentences are written. When the topic shifts to a new facet, then an indent acknowledges that.

Reveal the 3 Common Reasons to Indent a Paragraph:

1. Subtopic Shift. When the facts, information, details, or ideas shift to another facet of the topic, it's time for a new paragraph. Indent when a new character or person is introduced. Indent for each new event or happening. Reveal example paragraphs from recently read mentor text. Describe the subtopic of one paragraph and the subtopic of the next one. Define that as a shift in information and rationale for a paragraph break.

2. Setting Shift. When there is a shift in time, location, day, or date, writers alert their readers with an indent. Think of it like a video camera. When a different scene or setting is in the viewfinder, then there should have been a paragraph break. A more abstract facet of setting is mood. But when the mood or emotional energy changes, it usually requires a paragraph break, too.

3. Speaker Shift. Every time a character (dialogue) or individual (quote) speaks, a new paragraph is needed. When every line of a back-and-forth conversation isn't labeled with a speaker, the reader still knows who is talking because of this paragraph rule. There should also be a new paragraph when the writing goes from a character/expert quote back to the body paragraphs/narrator.

Independent Writing: Return to previous drafts and proofread for missing indents. Add the paragraph symbol and label subtopic, setting, or speaker to indicate the reason for the paragraph break.

entries.complete_ml_text:
Launching the Writer's Workshop: Grades 3-12 — Section 13: Teaching Conventions, Mini-Lesson #4: Apply quotation marks around speech

Much of a story is presented by a narrator — the person describing the event. However, occasionally characters "talk." Within informative, persuasive, and argumentative writing, the author (the student) presents his ideas/thinking with the occasional expert quote included.

This juggling of "speakers" can confuse the reader if convention rules aren't followed. Writers must indicate to their readers when someone besides the author or narrator is "talking."

Review the evolution of a quotation mark. In Greek times, playwrights did not use quote marks to tell the actor what to say. Quote marks hadn't been "invented" yet. Rather, the writers drew a pair of lips around the words an actor was to say. These lips represented an actor opening his mouth and speaking. Playwrights drew a second pair of lips to indicate when the speaking part was over and the actor should close his mouth.

Eventually a shorthand version was created — the quotation marks. Present-day quotation marks represent the pair of lips. The left one indicates the mouth/lips open and the right set concludes the speaking with the closing of the mouth/lips.

Only the words that come out of a character or expert's mouth are within the "lip" marks. The adjacent words and phrases that indicate who said it and/or how it was said are not to be included in the quotation marks. These descriptions are provided by the author/narrator. They are known as speaker tags and attribution. Since these phrases were not actually spoken out of the character or expert's lips, then they are not to be included within the quotation marks.

The accurate application of quotation marks is an unspoken agreement between readers and writers. When students don't follow this writing rule, the reader struggles to differentiate between what was said by the narrator/author versus characters/experts.

Independent Writing: Students sit in teams of three. Provide passages from mentor text that include a combination of quotations and narration. Students decide who's character A, who's character B, and who's the narrator. They read the excerpt aloud, depending on the speaker. Each time character A or B speaks, that student will also make air quotes to signal the opening and closing of his mouth.

entries.complete_ml_text:
PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #1: Recognize opinion topics — Kindergarten

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that writers share stories and teach information. But writers can also share what they think or believe. Today, I'm going to teach you how to tell when writing is sharing an opinion — or not.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing starts with an opinion. An opinion tells what the writer thinks, feels, or believes about a topic that has different sides or choices. Facts are right or wrong — but opinions are not. They are simply different. People can think and feel differently about the same topic. (Introduce the icons & hand gestures.)

When a reader recognizes that a piece of writing is persuasive, he understands: the writer is going to share what HE thinks and explain why his choice is best.

WHY the skill is important | If a reader cannot tell the difference between opinions and facts, he may confuse the writer's opinion with true information. When readers recognize persuasive writing, they understand: "This is what the author believes." Then they can read and decide whether or not to agree.

HOW the skill works | After reading a little bit of the text…
1. ASK: Is the author describing what happened to characters? If yes, then it's a narrative story.
2. ASK: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? If yes, then it's informative writing.
3. ASK: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings on a topic? Look for opinion words like "I think, my favorite, the best." Ask yourself: Could someone have a different opinion on this same topic? If yes, then it's persuasive writing.

This is how readers determine if a writer is revealing a story, telling facts, or sharing his opinion.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I figure out what type of writing this is. Project Lunch Text A and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a main character. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "Lunch is a time to eat during the school day." That's a fact. "Lunch gives your body energy." Everyone agrees with that. Hmm… Everything here sounds like true information. But let me check one more question before I decide.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings about a topic? Let me look for opinion words like — I think, I feel, the best. (Scan slowly, pointing.) I don't see any. The author is simply describing lunch. Shake head. This is NOT persuasive.
So it's definitely not a story or an opinion. This text includes facts everyone agrees on. This is informative writing.

OK, I'm going to do this again. I'm going to determine if the author is sharing an opinion with me/the reader. Project Lunch Text B and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a character or a problem. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "You get to eat yummy food." Hmm — is "yummy" a fact? Not everyone thinks the same food is yummy. (Pause.) "After lunch you feel ready to learn." That seems like a fact — but I also know I sometimes feel sleepy after eating a big lunch. Hmm… I'm not sure. Let me check the third writing purpose.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings about a topic? Let me look for opinion words. (Point to the very first sentence.) "I think lunch is the best time at school." There it is — "I think." That is an opinion phrase and "best" is a sign this is a persuasive writing. The author is telling me what HE thinks, not what everyone agrees on. Someone could have a different opinion. Someone might think recess or art is the best time of the day. (Nod.) Since I can name a different opinion, this topic is definitely NOT informative. This is persuasive writing. The author is sharing what he thinks and trying to get me to agree.

Today, we are learning how to recognize the signals that reveal if an author is sharing his opinion — if he is writing persuasively.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. Project Family Text A. Read it aloud quickly. Do not ask students to comment.

Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say that you don't think it is… but then again "family" could be the character and "feeling sad" could be a problem. Hmm… let's move on to the next writing purpose and see if it helps us.

Reread "My family is very special to me" and "We have so much fun playing games and laughing." 2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? Do all families play games or is this author sharing about HIS family? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say it's not true for everyone. Let's look at another sentence. "Families are the best." Do you see any opinion words in that sentence? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say "best." So what type of writing is this? 1… 2… 3… Blurt! Persuasive — right!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to tell when a writer is sharing his opinion — or not. If we can recognize opinions, then we are closer to being able to write them.

During Independent Writing Time, your job is to read several short texts and apply the same process. You will mark the text with a "P" if you determine it's persuasive and shares an opinion. Mark an "I" if it's informative and teaches facts. Mark an "E" if it's an entertaining narrative story. Let's go be writers!

entries.complete_ml_text:
PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (1 of 2) — Kindergarten

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that persuasive writing is about choices — it's about picking a side and writing about what you think. But how do you pick which side to write about? Today, I'm going to teach you how to determine which side is the strongest.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing is more than just your opinion — it's the strongest opinion that you can prove. Writers don't "pick" a side right away. First they think carefully about both choices.

WHY the skill is important | The strongest side is the one you can say the most about. If you pick a side too fast, you might miss a stronger one. Thinking through both sides first helps you find the one with the most to say.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Look at your topic. What are the two choices? Don't pick yet — just name them.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. It's hard not to blurt out your favorite right away. (Demonstrate hand over your mouth.) We slow down and think first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Reveal the blue hat.) Writers put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best — even if your heart isn't there. (Teach students to use their hands and mime placing a hat on their heads.) When you've thought of everything you can for that side, take the hat off. Stop thinking like that person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Reveal the red hat but don't put it on yet.) You may have enjoyed thinking about the first side — but this one? Maybe not so much. But we have to pretend to love this side. We don't say "eww" or make faces. So you put on that hat and think their thoughts. (Introduce the gesture of picking up a hat, putting it on, thinking, taking it off, then switching to the other hat.)

Ask yourself: What is good about it? What would someone who loves this side say? Thinking like the other side is hard. Here are a couple writer tricks to help you.
• Close your eyes and picture a person — maybe someone you know — who would really love this choice. What do they like? Why would someone choose this? What would they say is good about it?
• Have you ever seen this topic/side in real life? A place, a person, a thing? What did you notice? That might help you think of more details that make someone like this.
• What have you heard about this topic/side? What have your friends, family, or teachers said about this?

Remember, you are only pretending to like this side. You're just borrowing that person's brain for a minute. Only after thinking through both sides carefully can a writer determine which one is stronger.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I think through both sides before I pick one.

Step 1: Name both sides. My topic is: Which is the better fast food restaurant — McDonald's or Taco Bell? (Display the McDonald's & Taco Bell T-Chart.) Those are my two choices. I'm not picking yet. I'm just naming them.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. My first thought is already in my head — but I'm not saying it yet. (Place hand over mouth.) I have to think through both sides first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I'm putting on my McDonald's thinking cap. I'm going to think like someone who really loves McDonald's — (whisper) which isn't hard because I really do love it. OH NO! (Slap hand over mouth.) OK… So I have to think of things great about McDonald's. It has those crispy fries. And Happy Meals with toys. And Playland where kids can run around. And McFlurries! And chicken nuggets. And breakfast all day. Wow! It's so easy to think of details when I love the choice. OK, I've thought of everything I can for this side. (Take the hat off.) I'm done thinking like a McDonald's person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Hold up the red hat but don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves Taco Bell. Hmm. (Make a neutral face — no "eww," no faces.) I don't really know much about Taco Bell. I haven't been there much. But I have to pretend to borrow someone else's brain. (Put on the red hat.) Let me close my eyes and picture those Taco Bell commercials — the ones with people biting into crunchy tacos piled high with toppings… who love that you can choose hard or soft shells… who gets excited about all the different sauces… who likes that Taco Bell feels different from every other fast food place — like it's got its own thing going on. (Lift hat slightly off your head and whisper.) I don't really like all that stuff, (put hat back on head), but someone who loves Taco Bell probably does. And that's what I'm doing, trying to think like someone who loves this choice.

Today, we are learning how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic so that we can eventually figure out the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example.
1. Name both sides. The topic is: What is the best season — summer or winter? (Display both sides. Point to each.) Two choices. We are not picking yet — just naming them.
2. Hand over mouth. You may already have a favorite but don't say it! (Hand over mouth.) We have to think through both sides first.
3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Summer thinking cap. What details come to mind for someone who loves summer? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard hot sunny days, swimming, ice cream, popsicles, no school. So many details! (Hat off — students mime.) OK, we've thought of many summer-is-the-best details.
4. Think like the other side. Now we have to think like someone who loves winter — even if you don't. (Red hat on — students mime.) Let's close our eyes and picture someone playing outside in winter. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard building a snowman, snowball fights, hot chocolate. What else is fun or good about winter? What events or holidays occur over the winter? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard go sledding, Christmas time, etc.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic before picking one.

During Independent Writing Time, you and your partner will think through which is better — indoor or outdoor recess. When I project a topic, put on your blue hat and together I want you & your partner to think every detail you can for that side. Then switch pretend hats and think like someone who loves the other side. See how many details you & your partner can come up with for each side. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (2 of 2) — Kindergarten

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Yesterday we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — putting on each thinking cap and pushing ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides. Today I'm going to teach you how to jot down the details you think of for each side. This will bring us one step closer to determining the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Yesterday we thought about both sides of a persuasive topic. But thinking alone isn't enough — if writers only think through details in their heads, those ideas slip away before they ever make it into writing.

Jotting captures each detail on paper during prewriting. Jotting means writing something down quickly and simply — just enough to remember the thinking. Kindergartners jot with a quick picture and a label word — not a detailed drawing. (Connect to research unit jotting if previously taught — SKILL 1, Days 2-3.) We used jotting before when we were doing research & collecting fact phrases from texts.

WHY the skill is important | If writers only think through details in their heads, ideas slip away. Jotting captures each detail on paper so it doesn't get lost.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Write one choice at the top of each side of the T-Chart. Write one choice next to the blue hat and one choice next to the red hat.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. Resist blurting out an opinion. We are going to THINK about both sides, one at a time.

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Reveal the blue hat.) Remember to put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. (Students mime placing a hat on their heads.) As you think of a detail, jot it in its own space on that side of the T-Chart. Writers put a quick picture and simple label to remind them of the detail they thought of. Then, when you think of another detail for that same side, write it below the one before it, stacking down that same side. All of the details for that one choice are on the same side.

If you fill up all the spaces on that side — don't stop and don't switch to the other side yet. Grab a second T-Chart and keep jotting on that same side. The other side stays empty for now — that's OK. You are still thinking like a blue hat person. Stay in that thinking cap until every detail is captured. (Remove blue hat. Students mime.)

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat. Students mime.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice. Use the same thinking strategies. Say each detail out loud. Then jot it (quick picture & word label) in its own space on that side of the T-Chart.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I jot details for both sides of my persuasive topic.

Step 1: Name both sides. Yesterday my topic was: Which is the better fast food restaurant — McDonald's or Taco Bell? (Display a blank T-Chart.) The first thing I have to do is write one choice at the top of each side. (Write McDonald's on the left. Write Taco Bell on the right.) There — both sides named.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. I already know which one I love — (hand over mouth) — but I'm jotting both sides first because that's what persuasive writers do.

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I've got my McDonald's thinking cap on. Yesterday I thought of several details that make McDonald's great. I need to rethink of them, one at a time, and jot them on the McDonald's side of the T-Chart.
• Crispy fries is a detail. (Draw while talking aloud.) I can draw a quick picture of fries using my pencil. I need to put it in the first box under the McDonald's side. And I'll label it "fries."
• (Look up and think.) I'm also thinking that McDonald's is great because of the Happy Meal. (Look down at the first detail and slide your finger to the next space below it.) I need to write this next McDonald's detail in the space below the first one. I have to keep all the McDonald's details on the same side. (Draw while talking aloud.) I can draw a box with a handle on it. I'll label it "Hap Meal." That's my jot. It's just a reminder of a detail I'll write in a sentence later.
• (Repeat with McFlurry. After the third detail, demonstrate what to do when one side is full.) Wow — I filled up this whole side! But wait — I just thought of something else — the Playland at McDonald's. (Look at the full T-Chart.) There are no more spaces on this side. Do I stop? No! I grab a second T-Chart. (Display a second T-Chart.) I write McDonald's at the top of this side too — because I'm still thinking like a McDonald's person. (Model drawing and labeling Playland.) OK, I've thought of everything I can for this side. (Take the hat off.) I'm done thinking like a McDonald's person.

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat.) I put on the thinking cap of someone who loves Taco Bell. (Point at T-Chart and the right side.) Any details I come up with now, will all go on the right side — under the words "Taco Bell." I'm picturing someone who loves crunchy tacos piled high with toppings.
• Draw a taco and write "taco."
• Draw a curved hard shell and a circle/soft shell. Write "shells."
• Draw a rectangle and label it "sauces."

Today, we are learning how to think & jot details for both sides of a persuasive topic. This is what writers do before determining the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Yesterday, you thought about: What is the best season — Summer or Winter? Help me jot down those details. (Reveal a new T-Chart.)

1. Name both sides. Where should I write "Summer?" Point in the air. Yes, right here next to the blue hat. And where do I write down the other choice — winter? Point in the air. Yep, right here by the red hat.

2. Hand over mouth.

3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — swimming, ice cream, popsicles, no school. (Model how to start a second T-Chart when one side gets full.)

4. Think like the other side. (Switch hats.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — building a snowman, snowball fights, hot chocolate, sledding.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think & jot down details for BOTH sides of a persuasive. This is an important step before we can determine the strongest side.

During Independent Writing Time, you will fill out a T-Chart for which is better — indoor or outdoor recess. This time you will work alone. (Yesterday you brainstormed with a partner. Today, you will jot down the details by yourself.) Think of all the details you can for one side before switching to the other side. And if you need a second T-Chart, I've got extra ones right here. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #3: Write an opinion — Kindergarten

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Up until now, everything we have done in our persuasive unit has fallen under prewriting. We've listed details for both sides and figured out the strongest one. Now it's time to start drafting — and the very first thing a persuasive writer does is tell the audience his opinion. Today, I'm going to teach you how to write out the opinion at the beginning of any persuasive writing.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
All writing has a beginning, middle, and end — like a train with an engine, middle cars, and a caboose. That's a complete train and complete writing.

WHAT the skill is | In persuasive writing, the engine is the opinion sentence. This is where the writer tells the reader which side he chose and what he thinks.

WHY the skill is important | The reader needs to know right away that the writer is sharing an opinion. Starting with an opinion sentence tells the reader: this is what I think. Without an opinion sentence at the beginning of persuasive, the reader doesn't know what side the writer is on.

HOW the skill works |
STEP 1. Name the strongest side. Look back at your T-Chart. Find the side circled. Find the word(s) written next to the hat (on the strongest side). Use that word or those words in the first sentence.

STEP 2. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. (Connect to SKILL #1 — opinion signal words.) These words signal to the reader that an opinion is coming. Choose 3 to test out in Step 3.

STEP 3. Put the two parts together. Say it in one sentence out loud: strongest side + opinion words. Name the strongest side AND one of the opinion words/phrases in one sentence.
• Then, say the strongest side again with a different opinion word/phrase.
• Try out a couple different sentences by saying them out loud.
• You are sharing the same opinion each time; you're just saying it a little differently. So listen to the different ways you come up with. Pick the one that is easiest to say and easiest to understand.
• The one that sounds the best is the sentence to write/draw.

STEP 4. Write the sentence. After reading this first sentence, the audience will know exactly WHAT the writer thinks.

(NOTE: Stop there. The first sentence only names the opinion. No details. No "because.")

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I write my opinion sentence.

STEP 1. Name the strongest side. I look back at my T-Chart. (Point to the T-Chart.) I circled this side — McDonald's. That was my strongest side. It had the most details, the most proof. (Point to the word "McDonald's" next to the blue hat.) That's the word I need in my first sentence.

STEP 2. Choose 3 opinion words or phrases. Now I need to pick 3 opinion words/phrases to try out. (Point to the opinion word anchor chart.) I'm going to try these — "My favorite…, I think…, I like…" (Write on the board.)

STEP 3. Put the two parts together. Now I put the two parts together — one of the opinion phrases plus "McDonald's," the strongest side. I'm going to try all three out loud and see which one sounds best.
• "My favorite…" + McDonald's. (Pause & think.) "My favorite fast food restaurant is McDonald's." Hmm. That sounds like a complete sentence. I like it — but let me try the next one.
• "I think…" + McDonald's. (Pause & think.) "I think McDonald's is the best fast food restaurant." Ooh — that sounds strong. And I used "best" — that's another opinion word. I'll try one more way to say my opinion.
• "I like…" + McDonald's. (Pause & think.) "I like McDonald's better than any other fast food restaurant." That's OK — but it doesn't feel as strong as the first two.

(Review the first two choices again, saying them to yourself out loud.) I think I like the second one best — "I think McDonald's is the best fast food restaurant." It sounds strong. It sounds like an opinion. And it tells my reader exactly which side I chose.

STEP 4. Write the sentence. So now I need to write my opinion. This will be my very first sentence on lined paper. (Write slowly while narrating: I… think… McDonald's… is… the… best… fast… food… restaurant.) (Put the pencil/marker down.) And I stop. Right there. No because. No details. My reader knows what I think. The beginning is just my opinion.

Today, we are learning how to use our T-Charts and opinion words to write the beginning sentence of any persuasive writing.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. (Reveal the T-Chart of best season — summer or winter?)

1. Name the strongest side. Which side did we determine was the strongest yesterday? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Yes, summer! How do you know? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Right, because it has the most details. So we want to use the word "summer" in our opinion sentence.

2. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Look at the anchor chart. We also need to choose some opinion words from the chart. How about: "My favorite…, I think…, The best…"

3. Put the two parts together. Now it's time to put those two parts together — "summer" and "My favorite." Let's try each one out loud. Which one sounds strongest?
• "My favorite…" + Summer. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "My favorite season is summer."
• "I think…" + Summer. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "I think summer is the best season."
• "The best…" + Summer. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "The best season is summer."

Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I agree, "I think summer is the best season" is a clear opinion. That's the first sentence to write in your persuasive.

Today, we are learning how to use opinion words and our strongest side from the T-Chart to write the first sentence of our persuasive piece.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
During Independent Writing Time, you will get out your T-Chart on which is better — indoor or outdoor recess? I want you to follow the same process that I just taught you: 1. Name the strongest side. 2. Choose 3 opinion words. 3. Put the parts together. I want you to write 3 opinion sentences — each one using a different opinion word with the strongest side. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #1: Recognize opinion topics — Grade 1

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that writers share stories and teach information. But writers can also share what they think or believe. Today, I'm going to teach you how to tell when writing is sharing an opinion — or not.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing starts with an opinion. An opinion tells what the writer thinks, feels, or believes about a topic that has different sides or choices. Facts are right or wrong — but opinions are not. They are simply different. People can think and feel differently about the same topic. (Introduce the icons & hand gestures.)

When a reader recognizes that a piece of writing is persuasive, he understands: the writer is going to share what HE thinks and explain why his choice is best.

WHY the skill is important | If a reader cannot tell the difference between opinions and facts, he may confuse the writer's opinion with true information. When readers recognize persuasive writing, they understand: "This is what the author believes." Then they can read and decide whether or not to agree.

HOW the skill works | After reading a little bit of the text…
1. ASK: Is the author describing what happened to characters? If yes, then it's a narrative story.
2. ASK: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? If yes, then it's informative writing.
3. ASK: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings on a topic? Look for opinion words like "I think, my favorite, the best." Ask yourself: Could someone have a different opinion on this same topic? If yes, then it's persuasive writing.

This is how readers determine if a writer is revealing a story, telling facts, or sharing his opinion.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I figure out what type of writing this is. Project Bike Riding Text A and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a main character. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "People ride bikes on streets, sidewalks, or trails." That's a fact. "You use your legs to pedal." That's a fact — everyone agrees on that. "Wearing a helmet helps keep you safe." Yep, that's right. "Bikes can have two wheels or three wheels." Fact. I'm pretty sure this is informative writing, but I can check it by asking question 3.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings about a topic? Let me look for opinion words like — I think, I feel, I believe, the best. (Scan slowly, pointing.) I don't see any. And he's not taking a side. This is NOT persuasive.
So it's definitely not a story or an opinion. This text includes facts everyone agrees on. This is informative writing.

OK, I'm going to do this again; I'm going to determine if the author is sharing an opinion with me/the reader. Project Bike Riding Text B and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a character or a problem. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "You can go fast." Is that a fact? Not every bike rider goes fast. "Riding a bike is a great thing to do." Is that a fact everyone agrees on? What if someone doesn't know how to ride a bike? What if someone doesn't enjoy it? This doesn't feel like facts that EVERYONE agrees on. Let me check one more question.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings about a topic? (Point to the last sentence.) "Riding a bike is one of the best things you can do." Is "great" an opinion word? It's not "I think" or "I believe" — but "great" is telling me what the author thinks. Not everyone agrees that bike riding is great. Someone might think swimming or running is greater than bike riding exercise. So this topic has different choices. And even without saying "I think," the author is sharing what HE believes. This is persuasive writing.

Today, we are learning how to recognize the signals that reveal if an author is sharing his opinion — if he is writing persuasively.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. Project Library Text A. Read it aloud quickly. Do not ask students to comment.

Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say that you don't think it is. The library could be a setting, but there are no characters or a problem. This is NOT a narrative. Let's move on to the next question.

Reread "The best ones are the funny stories and the books with cool facts." 2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? Are there funny stories and fact books in the library? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say yes, that is true. But let's look at the words "best" and "cool" in that same sentence. Are those fact words or feeling words? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say those were feelings, what the author thinks and feels about the library. So what type of writing is this? 1… 2… 3… Blurt! Persuasive — right!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to tell when a writer is sharing his opinion — or not. If we can recognize opinions, then we are closer to being able to write them.

During Independent Writing Time, your job is to read several short texts and apply the same process. You will mark the text with a "P" if you determine it's persuasive and shares an opinion. Mark an "I" if it's informative and teaches facts. Mark an "E" if it's an entertaining narrative story. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (1 of 2) — Grade 1

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that persuasive writing is about choices — it's about picking a side and writing about what you think. But how do you pick which side to write about? Today, I'm going to teach you how to determine which side is the strongest.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing is more than just your opinion — it's the strongest opinion that you can prove. Writers don't "pick" a side right away. First they think carefully about both choices.

WHY the skill is important | The strongest side is the one you can say the most about. If you pick a side too fast, you might miss a stronger one. Thinking through both sides first helps you find the one with the most to say.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Look at your topic. What are the two choices? Don't pick yet — just name them.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. It's hard not to blurt out your favorite right away. (Demonstrate hand over your mouth.) We slow down and think first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Reveal the blue hat.) Writers put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best — even if your heart isn't there. (Teach students to use their hands and mime placing a hat on their heads.) When you've thought of everything you can for that side, take the hat off. Stop thinking like that person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Reveal the red hat but don't put it on yet.) You may have enjoyed thinking about the first side — but this one? Maybe not so much. But we have to pretend to love this side. We don't say "eww" or make faces. So you put on that hat and think their thoughts. (Introduce the gesture of picking up a hat, putting it on, thinking, taking it off, then switching to the other hat.)

Ask yourself: What is good about it? What would someone who loves this side say? Thinking like the other side is hard. Here are a couple writer tricks to help you.
• Close your eyes and picture a person — maybe someone you know — who would really love this choice. What do they like? Why would someone choose this? What would they say is good about it?
• Have you ever seen this topic/side in real life? A place, a person, a thing? What did you notice? That might help you think of more details that make someone like this.
• What have you heard about this topic/side? What have your friends, family, or teachers said about this?

Remember, you are only pretending to like this side. You're just borrowing that person's brain for a minute. Only after thinking through both sides carefully can a writer determine which one is stronger.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I think through both sides before I pick one.

Step 1: Name both sides. My topic is: What is the best pet — dog or cat? (Display the dog & cat T-Chart.) Those are my two choices. I'm not picking yet. I'm just naming them.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. My first thought is already in my head — but I'm not saying it yet. (Place hand over mouth.) I have to think through both sides first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I'm putting on my Dog thinking cap. I'm going to think like someone who really loves dogs — (whisper) which isn't hard because I really do love them. (Oops — slap hand over mouth.) OK… I have to think of things that are great about dogs. They snuggle with you. They wag their tails when they're happy. You can take them on walks. They play fetch. They lick you. They do tricks. They sleep right next to you — or even with you. And they bark at strangers to keep you safe!

Wow! It's so easy to think of details when I love the choice. (Take the hat off.) OK, I've thought of everything I can for dogs. I'm done thinking like a dog person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Hold up the red hat but don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves cats. Hmm. (Make a neutral face — no "eww," no faces.) Cats aren't really my thing — but I have to pretend to borrow someone else's brain. (Put on the red hat.) Let me close my eyes and picture someone who loves their cat… who loves how soft and fluffy that fur is… who thinks it's so cute when a cat curls up and purrs… who loves watching their cat leap up high and chase a toy across the floor… who appreciates that cats are quiet and calm and don't need walks… (Lift hat slightly off your head and whisper.) Cats aren't really for me, (put hat back on head), but someone who loves cats probably thinks all of that is the best. And that's what I'm doing — thinking like someone who loves this choice.

Today, we are learning how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic so that we can eventually figure out the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example.
1. Name both sides. The topic is: Which is better — indoor or outdoor recess? (Display both sides. Point to each.) Two choices. We are not picking yet — just naming them.
2. Hand over mouth. You may already have a favorite but don't say it! (Hand over mouth.) We have to think through both sides first.
3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Indoor-Recess thinking cap. What details come to mind for someone who loves that? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard toys in cupboard, build towers with Legos, draw & color, play board games, etc. (If students lack background knowledge, apply the strategies introduced earlier.) OK, we've thought of many indoor-recess details. (Hat off — students mime.)
4. Think like the other side. Now we have to think like someone who loves outdoor recess. (Red hat on — students mime.) Let's close our eyes and picture someone playing outside at recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard play tag, swing on swings, go down slide, hang on monkey bars, play with friends in other classes, etc.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic before picking one.

During Independent Writing Time, you and your partner will think through which is better — playing on the monkey bars or the swings. When I project a topic, put on your blue hat and together I want you & your partner to think every detail you can for that side. Then switch pretend hats and think like someone who loves the other side. See how many details you & your partner can come up with for each side. Let's go be writers!

Today I'm going to teach you how to jot down the details you think of for each side. This will bring us one step closer to determining the strongest side.

We jot a couple words — and a quick picture if we need to. (Connect to research unit jotting if previously taught — SKILL 1, Days 2-3.) We used jotting before when we were doing research & collecting fact phrases from texts.

WHY the skill is important | If writers only think through details in their heads, ideas slip away. Jotting captures each detail on paper so it doesn't get lost.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Write one choice at the top of each side of the T-Chart. Write one choice next to the blue hat and one choice next to the red hat.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. Resist blurting out an opinion. We are going to THINK about both sides, one at a time.

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Reveal the blue hat.) Remember to put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. (Students mime placing a hat on their heads.) Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat. Students mime.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice. Use the same thinking strategies. Say each detail out loud. Then jot it on its own line on that side of the T-Chart.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I jot details for both sides of my persuasive topic.

Step 1: Name both sides. Yesterday my topic was: What is the best pet — dog or cat? (Display a blank T-Chart.) The first thing I have to do is write one choice at the top of each side. (Write dog on the left & cat on the right.) There — both sides are named.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. I already know which one I love — (hand over mouth) — but I'm jotting both sides first because that's what persuasive writers do.

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I've got my Dog thinking cap on. Yesterday I thought of several details that make dogs a great pet. I need to rethink of them, one at a time, and jot them on the Dog side of the T-Chart. Dogs snuggle with you — that's a detail. I need to jot it on the first line under Dog.

(Look up and think.) Dogs wag their tails when they're happy. (Slide finger to the next line below.) Next detail goes right below the first one — same side. (Jot "wag tail.")
• Repeat with fetch and lick.

(After the fourth detail, demonstrate what to do when one side is full.) Wow — I filled up this whole side! But wait — I just thought of another one — dogs do tricks! (Look at the full T-Chart.) There are no more lines on this side. Do I stop? No! I grab a second T-Chart. (Display a second T-Chart.) I write Dog at the top of this side too — because I'm still thinking like a Dog person. (Model how to jot "do tricks.")

OK, I've thought of everything I can for this side. (Take the hat off.) I'm done thinking like a Dog person.

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat.) I put on the thinking cap of someone who loves Cats. (Point at T-Chart and the right side.) Any details I come up with now, will all go on the right side — under the word "Cat."
• I'm picturing someone who loves how soft and fluffy that fur is. (Jot "soft fur.")
• I'm picturing someone who loves when a cat curls up and purrs. (Jot "curls up, purr.")
• I'm picturing someone who loves watching their cat leap up and chase a toy. (Jot "leaps in air.")

Cats aren't really for me — but someone who loves cats would say all of that is the best.

Today, we are learning how to think & jot details for both sides of a persuasive topic. This is what writers do before determining the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Yesterday, you thought about: What is better — indoor or outdoor recess? Help me jot down those details. (Reveal a new T-Chart.)

1. Name both sides. Where should I write "Indoor?" Point in the air. Yes, right here next to the blue hat. And where do I write down the other choice — "Outdoor?" Point in the air. Yep, right here by the red hat.

2. Hand over mouth.

3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — toys, Lego towers, color, board games, etc. (Model how to start a second T-Chart when one side gets full.)

4. Think like the other side. (Switch hats.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — swing on swings, go down slide, hang on monkey bars, play with friends in other classes, etc.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think & jot down details for BOTH sides of a persuasive. This is an important step before we can determine the strongest side.

During Independent Writing Time, you will fill out a T-Chart for which is better — indoor or outdoor recess. This time you will work alone. (Yesterday you brainstormed with a partner. Today, you will jot down the details by yourself.) Think of all the details you can for one side before switching to the other side. And if you need a second T-Chart, I've got extra ones right here. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #3: Write an opinion — Grade 1

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Up until now, everything we have done in our persuasive unit has fallen under prewriting. We've listed details for both sides and figured out the strongest one. Now it's time to start drafting — and the very first thing a persuasive writer does is tell the audience his opinion. Today, I'm going to teach you how to write out the opinion at the beginning of any persuasive writing.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
All writing has a beginning, middle, and end — like a train with an engine, middle cars, and a caboose. That's a complete train and complete writing.

WHAT the skill is | In persuasive writing, the engine is the opinion sentence. This is where the writer tells the reader which side he chose and what he thinks.

WHY the skill is important | The reader needs to know right away that the writer is sharing an opinion. Starting with an opinion sentence tells the reader: this is what I think. Without an opinion sentence at the beginning of persuasive, the reader doesn't know what side the writer is on.

HOW the skill works |
STEP 1. Name the strongest side. Look back at your T-Chart. Find the side circled. Find the word(s) written next to the hat (on the strongest side). Use that word or those words in the first sentence.

STEP 2. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. (Connect to SKILL #1 — opinion signal words.) These words signal to the reader that an opinion is coming. Choose 3 to test out in Step 3.

STEP 3. Put the two parts together. Say it in one sentence out loud: strongest side + opinion words. Name the strongest side AND one of the opinion words/phrases in one sentence.
• Then, say the strongest side again with a different opinion word/phrase.
• Try out a couple different sentences by saying them out loud.
• You are sharing the same opinion each time; you're just saying it a little differently. So listen to the different ways you come up with. Pick the one that is easiest to say and easiest to understand.
• The one that sounds the best is the sentence to write/draw.

STEP 4. Write the sentence. After reading this first sentence, the audience will know exactly WHAT the writer thinks.

(NOTE: Stop there. The first sentence only names the opinion. No details. No "because.")

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I write my opinion sentence.

STEP 1. Name the strongest side. I look back at my T-Chart. (Point to the T-Chart.) I circled this side — Dog. That was my strongest side. It had the most details, the most proof. (Point to the word "Dog" next to the blue hat.) That's the word I need in my first sentence.

STEP 2. Choose 3 opinion words or phrases. Now I need to pick 3 opinion words/phrases to try out. (Point to the opinion word anchor chart.) I'm going to try these — My favorite…, I think…, I like… (Write on the board.)

STEP 3. Put the two parts together. Now I put the two parts together — 1 of the opinion phrases plus "Dog," the strongest side. I'm going to try all three out loud and see which one sounds best.
• "My favorite…" + dog. (Pause & think.) "My favorite pet is a dog." Hmm. That sounds like a complete sentence. I like that, but let me try the next one to see if I like it any better.
• "I think…" + dog. (Pause & think.) "I think dogs are the best pet." Ooh — that sounds strong. And I used "best" — that's another opinion word. I'll try one more way to say my opinion.
• "I like…" + dog. (Pause & think.) "I like dogs better than any other pet." Hmm. That one is OK — but it doesn't have the strong opinion feeling like the first two did.

(Review the first two choices again, saying them to yourself out loud.) I think I like the second one best — "I think dogs are the best pet." It sounds strong. It sounds like an opinion. And it tells my reader exactly which side I chose.

STEP 4. Write the sentence. So now I need to write my opinion. This will be my very first sentence on lined paper. (Write slowly while narrating: I… think… dogs… are… the… best… pet.) (Put the pencil/marker down.) And I stop. Right there. No because. No details. My reader knows what I think. The beginning is just my opinion.

Today, we are learning how to use our T-Chart and opinion words to write the beginning sentence of any persuasive writing.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. (Reveal the T-Chart of best recess — outdoor or indoor.)

1. Name the strongest side. Which side did we determine was the strongest yesterday? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Yes — outdoor recess! How do you know? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Right, because it has the most details. So we want to use the words "outdoor recess" in our opinion sentence.

2. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Look at the anchor chart. We also need to choose some opinion words from the chart. How about: "I think…, I believe…, The best…"

3. Put the two parts together. Now it's time to put those two parts together.
• "I think…" + outdoor recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "I think outdoor recess is better than indoor recess."
• "I believe…" + outdoor recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "I believe outdoor recess is the best kind of recess."
• "The best…" + outdoor recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "The best recess is outdoor recess."

Which one sounds strongest? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I agree, "I think outdoor recess is better than indoor recess" is a clear, strong opinion. That's the first sentence to write in your persuasive.

Today, we are learning how to use opinion words and our strongest side from the T-Chart to write the first sentence of our persuasive piece.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
During Independent Writing Time, you will get out your T-Chart on which is better — monkey bars or swings? I want you to follow the same process that I just taught you: 1. Name the strongest side. 2. Choose 3 opinion words. 3. Put the parts together. I want you to write 3 opinion sentences — each one using a different opinion word with the strongest side. Let's go be writers!

entries.complete_ml_text:
PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #1: Recognize opinion topics — Grade 2

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that writers share stories (narratives) and teach information (via informatives) to their readers. But writers can also share their feelings, beliefs, and opinions. Today, I'm going to teach you how to tell if you're reading an opinion — or not.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing starts with an opinion. An opinion tells what the writer thinks, feels, or believes about a topic that has different sides or choices. Unlike facts — which are right or wrong — opinions are neither. They are simply different. Two people can read about the same topic and believe completely different things. (Introduce the icons & hand gestures.)

When a reader recognizes that a piece of writing is persuasive, he understands: the writer is going to share what HE thinks and explain why his choice is best.

WHY the skill is important | If a reader cannot tell the difference between opinions and facts, he may confuse what the writer believes with fact. Persuasive writing has a different purpose than informative writing. When readers recognize persuasive writing, they understand: "This is what the author believes." Then they can read and decide whether or not to agree.

HOW the skill works | After reading a little bit of the text…
1. ASK: Is the author describing what happened to characters? If yes, then it's a narrative story.
2. ASK: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? If yes, then it's informative writing.
3. ASK: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings on a topic? Look for opinion words like "I think, favorite, the best." Ask yourself: Could someone have a different opinion on this same topic? If yes, then it's persuasive writing.

This is how readers determine if a writer is revealing a story, telling facts, or sharing his opinion.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I figure out what type of writing this is. Project Lunch Text A and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a main character. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "School lunches offer a variety of food and drink choices." That's a fact. "These foods help give students energy for the rest of the day." Everyone agrees with that. "Choosing a balanced meal helps the body stay healthy." Yep — that's true information, too. Everything here sounds like facts everyone agrees on. But let me check the third writing purpose before I decide.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings about a topic? Let me look for opinion words like — I think, My favorite, always, the best. (Scan slowly, pointing.) I don't see any. And he's not taking a side. This is NOT persuasive.
So it's definitely not a story or an opinion. This text includes facts everyone agrees on. This is informative writing.

OK, I'm going to do this again. I'm going to determine if the author is sharing an opinion with me/the reader. Project Lunch Text B and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a character or a problem. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to the first sentence.) "Smoothies can include fruits like strawberries, bananas, and blueberries." That sounds like a fact. "These drinks provide important vitamins." That's probably true too. (Pause.) But wait — "Adding fresh fruit smoothies to the lunch menu would give students a healthy and refreshing option." Would everyone agree with that? Does every school need smoothies on the menu? That doesn't feel like something everyone agrees on. Let me think through the persuasive lens.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings about a topic? (Point to the first sentence again. Point/Reread the last sentence, too.) "Fresh fruit smoothies would be a smart addition to the lunch menu." Smart — I'm questioning if that's an opinion word? It's not "I think" or "I believe" — but "smart addition" is describing what the author thinks about this idea. Someone else might think water or milk is a better drink choice. So the author is trying to convince the reader to agree. This is persuasive writing.

Today, we are learning how to recognize the signals that reveal if an author is sharing his opinion — if he is writing persuasively.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. Project Recess Game Text A. Read it aloud quickly. Do not ask students to comment.

Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say no — there's no character and nothing is happening to anyone. Let's keep going.

2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? Point to "The game involves running, quick thinking, and teamwork." Is that true for everyone who plays tag? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say yes — that does sound like a fact about tag. Let's look at one more sentence before we decide. Point to "Tag is a great choice for a fun and active recess game." Do you see any opinion words in that sentence? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say "great." Does everyone agree that tag is the greatest recess game? Could someone think a different game is better? (Nod.) Hmm… so what type of writing is this? 1… 2… 3… Blurt! Persuasive — right!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to tell when a writer is sharing his opinion — or not. If we can recognize opinions, then we are closer to being able to write them.

During Independent Writing Time, your job is to read several short texts and apply the same process. You will mark the text with a "P" if you determine it's persuasive and shares an opinion. Mark an "I" if it's informative and teaches facts. Mark an "E" if it's an entertaining narrative story. Let's go be writers!
