PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (1 of 2) — Grade 2

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that persuasive writing is about choices — it's about picking a side and writing about what you think. But how do you pick which side to write about? Today, I'm going to teach you how to determine which side is the strongest.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing is more than just your opinion — it's the strongest opinion that you can prove. Writers don't "pick" a side right away. First they think carefully about both choices.

WHY the skill is important | The strongest side is the one you can say the most about. If you pick a side too fast, you might miss a stronger one. Thinking through both sides first helps you find the one with the most to say.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Look at your topic. What are the two choices? Don't pick yet — just name them.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. It's hard not to blurt out your favorite right away. (Demonstrate hand over your mouth.) We slow down and think first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Reveal the blue hat.) Writers put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best — even if your heart isn't there. (Teach students to use their hands and mime placing a hat on their heads.) When you've thought of everything you can for that side, take the hat off. Stop thinking like that person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Reveal the red hat but don't put it on yet.) You may have enjoyed thinking about the first side — but this one? Maybe not so much. But we have to pretend to love this side. We don't say "eww" or make faces. So you put on that hat and think their thoughts. (Introduce the gesture of picking up a hat, putting it on, thinking, taking it off, then switching to the other hat.)

Ask yourself: What is good about it? What would someone who loves this side say? Thinking like the other side is hard. Here are a couple writer tricks to help you.
• Close your eyes and picture a person — maybe someone you know — who would really love this choice. What do they like? Why would someone choose this? What would they say is good about it?
• Have you ever seen this topic/side in real life? A place, a person, a thing? What did you notice? That might help you think of more details that make someone like this.
• What have you heard about this topic/side? What have your friends, family, or teachers said about this?

Remember, you are only pretending to like this side. You're just borrowing that person's brain for a minute. Only after thinking through both sides carefully can a writer determine which one is stronger.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I think through both sides before I pick one.

Step 1: Name both sides. My topic is: What is the best treat — a candy bar or ice cream? (Display the candy bar & ice cream T-Chart.) Those are my two choices. I'm not picking yet. I'm just naming them.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. My first thought is already in my head — but I'm not saying it yet. (Place hand over mouth.) I have to think through both sides first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I'm putting on my Candy Bar thinking cap. Candy bars are just… good. (Long pause.) Hmm. That's not a detail. I need to think smaller. What exactly happens when you eat a candy bar? (Close eyes.) I'm imagining a candy bar in my hands. I unwrap it. Ahh… I smell the chocolate. That's a detail! And then I take a bite. Oooh… and sometimes there's yummy things inside. Like caramel that is gooey and stretchy. Or peanut butter that's creamy. Or nuts make it crunchy. Those are all details for why someone would love a candy bar. I'm done thinking like a candy bar person. (Take the hat off.)

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Hold up the red hat but don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves ice cream. I mean it's fine — but I don't personally love it. I definitely need to borrow someone else's brain. (Put on the red hat.) Let me close my eyes and picture someone who really loves ice cream. (Close eyes.) I can picture someone standing at an ice cream counter, totally excited, trying to choose between all those flavors… stacking two scoops on a waffle cone… licking it before it melts… adding hot fudge and sprinkles on a big sundae…

I need to keep going. I could think about what I've seen at ice cream stores. Like I've seen friends mix two flavors together in a swirl. I've heard people say they love trying new flavors. Oh, milkshakes are made from ice cream. That's a good thing.

Today, we are learning how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic so that we can eventually figure out the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example.
1. Name both sides. The topic is: Which is better — outdoor or indoor recess? (Display both sides. Point to each.) Two choices. We are not picking yet — just naming them.
2. Hand over mouth. You may already have a favorite but don't say it! (Hand over mouth.) We have to think through both sides first.
3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) With your Outdoor-Recess thinking cap on, what would someone who loves outdoor recess say? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard running, climbing, swings, slide, monkey bars, playing with a ball. But wait — what else can you say besides just the recess equipment? Think smaller. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard shouting and laughing, racing friends, playing with kids from other classes, having all that space to run. (Hat off — students mime.) See how thinking smaller gave us more details?
4. Think like the other side. Now we have to think like someone who loves indoor recess — even if that's not you. (Red hat on — students mime.) Close your eyes and picture someone who gets excited when it rains because that means recess is inside and what do you get to do? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard Legos, drawing, board games, puzzles, sitting wherever you want, playing house. Great thinking from both sides!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic before picking one.

During Independent Writing Time, you and your partner will think through Which season is best — summer or winter. When I project a topic, put on your blue hat and together I want you & your partner to think every detail you can for that side. Then switch pretend hats and think like someone who loves the other side. See how many details you & your partner can come up with for each side. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (2 of 2) — Grade 2

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Yesterday we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — putting on each thinking cap and pushing ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides. Today I'm going to teach you how to jot down the details you think of for each side. This will bring us one step closer to determining the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Yesterday we thought about both sides of a persuasive topic. But thinking alone isn't enough — if writers only think through details in their heads, those ideas slip away before they ever make it into writing. Jotting captures each detail on paper during prewriting. Jotting means writing something down quickly and simply — just enough to remember the thinking. We jot a couple words — and a quick picture if we need to. (Connect to research unit jotting if previously taught — SKILL 1, Days 2-3.) We used jotting before when we were doing research & collecting fact phrases from texts.

WHY the skill is important | If writers only think through details in their heads, ideas slip away. Jotting captures each detail on paper so it doesn't get lost.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Write one choice at the top of each side of the T-Chart. Write one choice next to the blue hat and one choice next to the red hat.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. Resist blurting out an opinion. We are going to THINK about both sides, one at a time.

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Reveal the blue hat.) Remember to put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. (Students mime placing a hat on their heads.) As you think of a detail, jot it on its own line on that side of the T-Chart. Writers jot a couple words — just enough to remind them of the detail they thought of. Then, when you think of another detail for that same side, write it below the one before it, stacking down that same side. All of the details for that one choice are on the same side.

If you fill up all the lines on that side — don't stop and don't switch to the other side yet. Grab a second T-Chart and keep jotting on that same side. The other side stays empty for now — that's OK. You are still thinking like a blue hat person. Stay in that thinking cap until every detail is captured. (Remove blue hat. Students mime.)

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat. Students mime.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice. Use the same thinking strategies. Say each detail out loud. Then jot it on its own line on that side of the T-Chart.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I jot details for both sides of my persuasive topic.

Step 1: Name both sides. Yesterday my topic was: What is the best treat — a candy bar or ice cream? (Display a blank T-Chart.) The first thing I have to do is write one choice at the top of each side. (Write candy bar on the left & ice cream on the right.) There — both sides are named.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. I already know which one I love — (hand over mouth) — but I'm jotting both sides first because that's what persuasive writers do.

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I've got my Candy bar thinking cap on. Yesterday I thought of several details that are great about candy bars. I need to rethink them, one at a time, and jot them on the Candy bar side of the T-Chart.

Chocolate melts in your mouth — that's a detail. I need to jot that under Candy Bar. But I also want to be quick about it. I use shorthand and abbreviations — just enough so I remember the detail: "choc melt in mouth."

(Look up and think.) Caramel inside is gooey and stretchy. (Slide finger below the previous detail.) Next detail goes right below the first one — same side. (Jot "caramel = gooey, stretchy.")
• Repeat with "creamy PB" and "crunchy nuts."

(At some point demonstrate what to do when one side is full.) Wow — I filled up this whole side! But wait — I just thought of another one — chocolate is sweet. (Look at the full T-Chart.) There is no more space on this side. Do I stop? No! I grab a second T-Chart. (Display a second T-Chart.) I write Candy bar at the top of this same side. (Model how to jot "sweet.")

OK, I've thought of everything I can for this side. (Take the hat off.) I'm done thinking like a person who loves Candy bars.

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat.) I put on the thinking cap of someone who loves ice cream. (Point at T-Chart and the right side.) Any details I come up with now, will all go on the right side — under "Ice cream."
• I'm picturing someone at the counter choosing a flavor. (Jot "many flavors.")
• I'm picturing someone who is licking his cone because it's starting to melt. (Jot "lick.")
• I'm picturing someone with different scoops. (Jot "stack scoops" and "try new flavors.")

Today, we are learning how to think & jot details for both sides of a persuasive topic. This is what writers do before determining the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Yesterday, you thought about: What is better — outdoor or indoor recess? Help me jot down those details. (Reveal a new T-Chart.)

1. Name both sides. Where should I write "Outdoor?" Point in the air. Yes, right here next to the blue hat. And where do I write down the other choice — "Indoor?" Point in the air. Yep, right here by the red hat.

2. Hand over mouth.

3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — toys, Lego towers, draw, board games, etc. (Model how to start a second T-Chart when one side gets full.)

4. Think like the other side. (Switch hats.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — swing on swings, go down slide, hang on monkey bars, play with friends in other classes, etc.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think & jot down details for BOTH sides of a persuasive. This is an important step before we can determine the strongest side.

During Independent Writing Time, you will fill out a T-Chart for Which season is best — Summer or Winter. This time you will work alone. (Yesterday you brainstormed with a partner. Today, you will jot down the details by yourself.) Think of all the details you can for one side before switching to the other side. And if you need a second T-Chart, I've got extra ones right here. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #3: Write an opinion — Grade 2

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Up until now, everything we have done in our persuasive unit has fallen under prewriting. We've listed details for both sides and figured out the strongest one. Now it's time to start drafting — and the very first thing a persuasive writer does is tell the audience his opinion. Today, I'm going to teach you how to write out the opinion at the beginning of any persuasive writing.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
All writing has a beginning, middle, and end — like a train with an engine, middle cars, and a caboose. That's a complete train and complete writing.

WHAT the skill is | In persuasive writing, the engine is the opinion sentence. This is where the writer tells the reader which side he chose and what he thinks.

WHY the skill is important | The reader needs to know right away that the writer is sharing an opinion. Starting with an opinion sentence tells the reader: this is what I think. Without an opinion sentence at the beginning of persuasive, the reader doesn't know what side the writer is on.

HOW the skill works |
STEP 1. Name the strongest side. Look back at your T-Chart. Find the side circled. Find the word(s) written next to the hat (on the strongest side). Use that word or those words in the first sentence.

STEP 2. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. (Connect to SKILL #1 — opinion signal words.) These words signal to the reader that an opinion is coming. Choose 3 to test out in Step 3.

STEP 3. Put the two parts together. Say it in one sentence out loud: strongest side + opinion words. Name the strongest side AND one of the opinion words/phrases in one sentence.
• Then, say the strongest side again with a different opinion word/phrase.
• Try out a couple different sentences by saying them out loud.
• You are sharing the same opinion each time; you're just saying it a little differently. So listen to the different ways you come up with. Pick the one that is easiest to say and easiest to understand.
• The one that sounds the best is the sentence to write/draw.

STEP 4. Write the sentence. After reading this first sentence, the audience will know exactly WHAT the writer thinks.

(NOTE: Stop there. The first sentence only names the opinion. No details. No "because.")

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I write my opinion sentence.

STEP 1. Name the strongest side. I look back at my T-Chart. (Point to the T-Chart.) I circled this side — Candy bar. That was my strongest side. It had the most details, the most proof. (Point to the word "Candy bar" next to the blue hat.) That's the word I need in my first sentence.

STEP 2. Choose 3 opinion words or phrases. Now I need to pick 3 opinion words/phrases to try out. (Point to the opinion word anchor chart.) I'm going to try these — My favorite…, best…, I like… (Write on the board.) I have a few choices. Let me try them out.

STEP 3. Put the two parts together. Now I put the two parts together — 1 of the opinion phrases plus "Candy bar," the strongest side. I'm going to try all three out loud and see which one sounds best.
• "best" + Candy bar. (Pause & think.) "The best treat is a candy bar." Pause. Hmm. That works. I like that, but let me try the next one to see if I like it any better.
• "My favorite…" + Candy bar. (Pause & think.) "My favorite treat is a candy bar." Ooh — I like that one too. I'll try one more way to say my opinion.
• "I like…" + Candy bar. (Pause & think.) "I like candy bars the best." Pause. That works too!

All three are opinion sentences. They all name my side. I think I like the second one. It sounds strong. It sounds like an opinion. And it tells my reader exactly which side I chose.

STEP 4. Write the sentence. So now I need to write my opinion. This will be my very first sentence on lined paper. (Write slowly while narrating: My… favorite… treat… is… a… candy… bar.) (Put the pencil/marker down.) And I stop. Right there. No because. No details. My reader knows what I think. The beginning is just my opinion.

Today, we are learning how to use our T-Chart and opinion words to write the beginning sentence of any persuasive writing.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. (Reveal the T-Chart of best recess — outdoor or indoor.)

1. Name the strongest side. Which side did we determine was the strongest yesterday? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Yes — outdoor recess! How do you know? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Right, because it has the most details. So we want to use the words "outdoor recess" in our opinion sentence.

2. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Look at the anchor chart. We also need to choose some opinion words from the chart. How about: "I think…, I believe…, The best…"

3. Put the two parts together. Now it's time to put those two parts together.
• "I think…" + outdoor recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "I think outdoor recess is better than indoor recess."
• "I believe…" + outdoor recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "I believe outdoor recess is the best kind of recess."
• "The best…" + outdoor recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "The best recess is outdoor recess."

Which one sounds strongest? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I agree, "I think outdoor recess is better than indoor recess" is a clear, strong opinion. That's the first sentence to write in your persuasive.

Today, we are learning how to use opinion words and our strongest side from the T-Chart to write the first sentence of our persuasive piece.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
During Independent Writing Time, you will get out your T-Chart on what is the best season — Summer or Winter? I want you to follow the same process that I just taught you: 1. Name the strongest side. 2. Choose 3 opinion words. 3. Put the parts together. I want you to write 3 opinion sentences — each one using a different opinion word with the strongest side. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #1: Recognize opinion topics — Grade 3

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that writers share stories (narratives) and teach information (via informatives) to their readers. But writers can also share their feelings, beliefs, and opinions. Today, I'm going to teach you how to tell if you're reading an opinion — or not.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing starts with an opinion. An opinion tells what the writer thinks, feels, or believes about a topic that has different sides or choices. Unlike facts — which are right or wrong — opinions are neither. They are simply different. Two people can read about the same topic and believe completely different things. (Introduce the icons & hand gestures.)

When a reader recognizes that a piece of writing is persuasive, he understands: the writer is going to share what HE thinks and explain why his choice is best.

WHY the skill is important | If a reader cannot tell the difference between opinions and facts, he may confuse what the writer believes with fact. This gets trickier in third grade — because persuasive writing actually includes facts, details, and real examples. The writer uses those facts to support his opinion. That means a persuasive piece can sound a lot like an informative piece. When readers recognize persuasive writing, they understand: "This is what the author believes — and he is using facts to convince me." Then they can read and decide whether or not to agree.

HOW the skill works | After reading a little bit of the text…
1. ASK: Is the author describing what happened to characters? If yes, then it's a narrative story.
2. ASK: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? If yes — it's informative writing. But remember — persuasive writing also includes facts. So if you see facts, don't stop there. Keep questioning the author's purpose.
3. ASK: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings AND occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (The facts are there to support the opinion, not replace it.) Also look for subtle opinion words & adjectives — words like "should/not, most, best, important, better, necessary." Could someone have a different opinion on this same topic? If yes — it's persuasive writing.

This is how readers determine whether the writer's purpose is to describe a narrative story, inform with facts, or persuade the audience with his opinion.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I figure out what type of writing this is. Project Art Text A and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a main character. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "First, an artist lightly sketches the basic shapes." That's a fact — that's how drawing works. "After that, they trace over the final lines and erase extra marks." Yep, that's true. "Following these steps helps create a neat and complete drawing." Everyone would agree with that. (Pause.) Everything here sounds like facts and steps everyone agrees on. But remember — persuasive writing also includes facts. So I'm going to double check that it is not persuasive.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings & occasionally stating facts and details to support it? Let me look for subtle opinion words. (Scan slowly, pointing to each sentence.) I don't see any opinion words. The author isn't taking a side — he's just explaining how to draw. (Shake head.) This is NOT persuasive. This is informative writing.

OK, I'm going to do this again. I'm going to determine the author's purpose for writing. Project Art Text B and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a character or a problem. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to the first sentence.) "Colored pencils allow for careful shading." That sounds like a fact. "Artists can also blend colors." True, that's something colored pencils do. (Pause.) But wait — just reading facts doesn't mean this is automatically informative writing. Let me think about this through the persuasive lens.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings & occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (Point to the first sentence.) "Adding more colored pencils would improve student artwork." Improve — is that an opinion word? Would everyone agree colored pencils improve artwork? (Point to the last sentence.) "More colored pencils would support stronger and more detailed art projects." Stronger — that's an opinion word. Not everyone agrees on what makes art stronger. (Pause.) And look at how the facts work — "easier to control than markers," "artists can blend colors." Those facts aren't just teaching me about colored pencils. They are supporting the opinion. The facts are there to convince me. AHA! It's persuasive!

Today, we are learning how to recognize the signals that indicate an author is sharing his opinion within persuasive writing.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. Project Beginning-of-the-Day Text A. Read it aloud quickly. Do not ask students to comment.

1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say no — there's no character and nothing is happening to anyone. Let's keep going.

2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? Point to "Students would not need to stop at lockers or cubbies" and "This would save time and reduce crowding." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say those sound like facts. But persuasive includes some facts, so let's keep asking.

3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings supported by facts? Point to "Keeping coats in the classroom would make morning routines more efficient." Do you see a subtle opinion word? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say "efficient." Could someone argue it creates more clutter and distraction? (Nod.) What's the purpose of "save time," "reduce crowding," "stay focused." To teach or convince us? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. So what type of writing is this? Persuasive — right!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to tell when a writer is sharing his opinion — or not. If we can recognize opinions, then we are closer to being able to write them.

During Independent Writing Time, your job is to read several short texts and apply the same process. You will mark the text with a "P" if you determine it's persuasive and shares an opinion. Mark an "I" if it's informative and teaches facts. Mark an "E" if it's an entertaining narrative story. Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (1 of 2) — Grade 3

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that persuasive writing isn't just about what you think — it's about what you can prove. But how do you know which side you can prove best before you start writing? Today, I'm going to teach you how to think through both sides of a topic to determine the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing is more than just your opinion — it's the strongest opinion you can prove. Writers don't pick a side right away and start writing. Instead, they determine the strongest side by carefully thinking through both choices before committing to one. The strongest side isn't necessarily the one you like best — it's the one you can prove best.

WHY the skill is important | If a writer picks a side too quickly — based only on gut feeling — he may choose the harder side to prove. And "harder to prove" means exactly that: when he sits down to write, he can't think of what to say. Thinking through both sides first helps you find the one that you have the most to say about. And in persuasive writing, it's all about convincing the reader, and you need A LOT of details to make your point.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Look at the persuasive topic and identify both choices. Don't lean either direction yet — just name them side by side and treat them equally.

Step 2: Zip it. Before thinking begins, run your finger across your lips — zip them shut. (Demonstrate the zipper gesture.) Your opinion is locked inside. It's not gone — it's just waiting. You are not allowed to unzip until you have thought carefully through BOTH sides. This is how writers avoid rushing to a decision.

STEP 3: Think like one side. (Reveal the blue hat.) Writers put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. Think like someone who genuinely loves this choice — even if you don't. (Teach students to use their hands and mime placing a hat on their heads.)

To generate strong details, try these strategies.
• Picture someone you know who would love this choice. What would they say is great about it?
• Think small — don't just say "it's fun" or "it's good." Ask yourself: what exactly happens? What does it look, feel, smell, taste, or sound like? Small specific details are always stronger than big general ones.
• Think about what you've seen or heard — a commercial, a conversation, something a friend or family member said. That counts as thinking.

When you've thought of everything you can for that side, take the hat off. (Introduce the gesture of picking up a hat, putting it on, thinking, taking it off, then switching to the other hat.)

STEP 4: Think like the other side. (Take off the blue hat and put on the red one.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice — even if it's not your favorite. Use the same three strategies. Give this side the same honest effort you gave the first one. Your zipper stays shut until you've done both.

This is how writers determine the strongest side — by thinking through both before choosing.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I do this.

Step 1: Name both sides. My topic is: Would you rather stay up late or sleep in late? (Display the choices within a T-Chart.) Those are my two choices. I'm not picking yet — just naming them.

Step 2: Zip it. My first thought is already in my head. (Run finger across lips — zip.) Locked. Not saying it yet. I have to think through both sides first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I'm putting on the Stay Up Late thinking cap. I'm going to think like someone who really loves staying up late. OK… let me think small. What actually happens when you stay up late? Everyone else is asleep — so the whole house is quiet and it's all yours. Ummm, you can also play video games without anyone telling you to stop. You can finish a level you've been stuck on all day. You can watch shows you normally can't because it's past bedtime. There's something kind of cool about being up when everyone else isn't. I'm not really into it, but someone who liked staying up late might get excited about the dark sky full of stars. That's another detail for this side. Wow — once I started thinking small, the details just kept coming. (Take the hat off.) I'm done thinking like a stay-up-late person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Hold up the red hat but don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves sleeping in late. I don't know much about this side. I'm a morning person — but I have to zip it and borrow someone else's brain. I have to pretend to think like someone who does know about this. (Put on the red hat.)

Let me picture someone who loves sleeping in. They wake up when their body is ready — no alarm, no one shaking them awake. They just… open their eyes naturally. (Pause.) That's one detail. Let me think smaller. They're still warm under the blankets. The sun is already up so the room feels bright and cozy — not dark and groggy. They have so much energy because they actually slept enough.

What else? No rushing to the bathroom before everyone else. No long bus ride. Breakfast isn't rushed. The whole morning feels calm. (Pause and think.) And what have I heard people say about sleeping in? I've heard adults say it's the best feeling in the world — waking up with nowhere to be.

Today, we are learning how to push ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides — even the side we don't know well or wouldn't naturally choose — so we can find the side we can best prove.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example.
1. Name both sides. The topic is: What is the best pet — a dog or a cat?
2. Zip it. Locked. Think first.
3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Dog thinking cap. Don't just say "dogs are fun." Think small — what exactly does a dog DO that makes them a fun pet? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard wag their tails when they're happy, lick your face, tilt their head like they're really listening, do silly things that make you laugh. (Hat off — students mime.)
4. Think like the other side. (Red hat on — students mime.) Now think like a cat person — even if that's not you. Think small. Picture someone who loves their cat. What exactly does that cat do that makes them love it? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard purring on your lap, tiny pink noses, little paws, chasing a laser light across the floor. See how thinking small makes even the side you didn't expect feel full of details?

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — pushing ourselves to think small and find specific details, even for the side we wouldn't naturally choose.

During Independent Writing Time, you and your partner will think through both sides of this topic: Which is the best recess equipment — monkey bars or swings? When I project the topic, work with your partner to think of every small, specific detail you can for one side. Then switch hats and do the same for the other side. How many details can you two come up with? Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (2 of 2) — Grade 3

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Yesterday we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — putting on each thinking cap and pushing ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides. Today I'm going to teach you how to jot down the details you think of for each side. This will bring us one step closer to determining the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Yesterday you thought through both sides of a persuasive topic. But thinking alone isn't enough — ideas that stay in your head slip away before they ever make it into writing. Jotting captures each detail on paper during prewriting. Jotting means writing a concise phrase — 1-4 words to preserve the thinking without slowing down the process. (Connect to research unit jotting if previously taught — Skill 1, Day 2. Review shortcuts and abbreviations.)

WHY the skill is important | A persuasive writer's goal isn't just to list details — it's to jot as many details for BOTH sides as he can think of during prewriting. This is critical to determining the strongest side.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Write one choice at the top of each side of the T-Chart — blue hat side on the left, red hat side on the right. Both sides start equal.

Step 2: Zip it. (Zipper gesture — students mime.) Lock in your first instinct. Don't let it out yet. A writer who commits too early may miss the stronger argument entirely.

STEP 3: Think like one side & jot. (Reveal the blue hat. Students mime.) Put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. Jot each detail in 1–4 words, on its own line, & stacking it down that side. Writers typically begin with one side and continue until ideas slow.

If you fill every line on that side before you're finished thinking — grab a second T-Chart and continue on the same side. The other side stays empty for now. Stay in that thinking cap until every detail is captured. (Remove blue hat. Students mime.)

STEP 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat. Students mime.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice. Jot each detail on its own line, stacking down that side. Give this side the same honest effort.

Writers typically begin with one side and continue until ideas slow down. However, sometimes while making the second list (Side B), the writer has a new thought for Side A. No problem. Jump over to Side A and jot it. Then return to Side B and continue listing details.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I jot details for both sides of my persuasive topic.

Step 1: Name both sides. Yesterday my topic was: Would you rather stay up late or sleep in late? (Display a blank T-Chart.) I write one choice at the top of each side. (Write Stay Up Late on the left & Sleep In Late on the right.) There — both sides are named.

Step 2: Zip it. (Run finger across lips — zip.)

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I've got my Stay Up Late thinking cap on. Yesterday I thought of several details for this side. Now I jot them — 1–4 words each, stacking down the left side.

(Jot while narrating details.)
• Quiet house — all asleep
• Gaming — no one stops you
• Level up — took all day
• Watch late night shows
• Dark sky — stars, kind of cool

Once I started jotting, the details stacked up fast. (Take the hat off.) I think I'm done thinking like a stay-up-late person.

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Hold up the red hat — don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves sleeping in & jot down the detail. This is definitely harder for me because I'm such an early-morning person. But I'll think LIKE someone who loves to sleep in. (Put on the red hat.) Any details I come up with now, will all go on the right side — under "Sleep in late." (Point at T-Chart.)

• I picture someone waking up when their body is ready — no alarm. (Jot: "no alarm.")
• Still warm under the blankets. (Jot: "warm blankets.")
• Sun already up — bright and cozy. (Jot: "sun up, cozy.")
• Full of energy because you actually slept long enough. (Jot: "full/energy — slept enough.")

(Pause.) Wait — I just thought of something for the Stay Up Late side. (Switch hats.) Being up when everyone else is asleep means you're totally on your own. You're in charge. I have to jump back to Side A and capture that before I lose it. (Jot "on own, in charge.")

OK — back to Sleep In Late. (Switch hats again.)
• No rushing to the bathroom, or to catch the bus. Even breakfast isn't rushed. (Jot: "no rush — bath, bus, brkfst.")
• Whole morning feels calm. (Jot: "calm.")

Today, we are learning how to jot details for both sides of a persuasive topic — capturing specific details on paper so we can eventually determine the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Yesterday, you thought about: What is the best pet — a dog or a cat? Help me jot down those details. (Reveal a new T-Chart.)

1. Name both sides. Point in the air — where do I write down the two sides, the two choices? Yes, Dog by the blue hat & Cat by the red hat.

2. Zip it. Locked. Think first.

3. Think like one side & jot. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — wag tail = happy, lick face, tilt head = listening, etc.

4. Think like the other side & jot. (Switch hats.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — purr on lap, cuddle, tiny pink nose, jump high/across furniture, etc. Does any of this make you think of another detail about Dogs? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard some of you say dogs jump on you, too. I'll switch hats and jot that down before returning back to the Cats list.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think & jot down details for BOTH sides of a persuasive. This is an important step before we can determine the strongest side.

During Independent Writing Time, you will fill out a T-Chart for what is the best recess equipment — monkey bars or swings. This time you will work alone. (Yesterday you brainstormed with a partner. Today, you will jot down the details by yourself.) Think of all the details you can for one side before switching to the other side. And if you need a second T-Chart, I've got extra ones right here. Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #3: Write an opinion — Grade 3

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Up until now, everything we have done in our persuasive unit has been prewriting — thinking through both sides and determining the strongest one. Today we transition from prewriting to drafting. The first thing a persuasive writer does in his draft is tell the audience which side he has chosen. Today, I'm going to teach you how to write a strong opinion statement at the beginning of any persuasive piece.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing begins with an opinion statement. The first sentence tells the audience exactly what the writer thinks and which side he has chosen. This is no longer prewriting — this is the moment the writer goes public with his thinking.

WHY the skill is important | Without a clear opinion statement at the opening, the reader has no anchor — he doesn't know what side the writer is on or what the writing is trying to prove. By stating the opinion first, the writer signals his position immediately and sets up everything that follows. Remember — the goal of persuasive writing is to convince the audience to agree. So get to the point fast.

HOW the skill works |
STEP 1. Name the strongest side. Look back at your T-Chart. Find the side circled — the one with the most details and proof. The word or words labeling that side belong in your opinion sentence.

STEP 2. Name the bigger topic. This is typically found in the writing prompt. It's the broader subject the two sides come from — usually 1–3 words. It gives the reader context so the opinion doesn't appear out of nowhere.

STEP 3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. (Connect to SKILL #1 — opinion signal words.) By intermediate grades, writers rarely use "I think" or "I believe" in persuasive writing. Opinion language is much more subtle. It's drops a single word — like "should, clearly, or best" — rather than a sentence starter. Test out 3 different opinion words as options for the first sentence.

STEP 4. Put the 3 parts together. Combine all 3 items in one oral sentence: strongest side + bigger topic + opinion word. Try it different ways, each time using different opinion language. Listen for the version that is most direct, most confident, and most specific. The stronger and more precise that opening statement, the more confident and convincing the entire piece feels from the first sentence forward.

STEP 5. Write the sentence. The one that sounds the best is the sentence to write. This is how all persuasive writing should begin — with a clear, confident opinion statement that the rest of the writing will prove.

(NOTE: Stop there. The first sentence only names the opinion. No details. No "because." See SKILL #5 for where the "because" fits in persuasive writing.)

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I write an opinion sentence.

Step 1: Name the strongest side. I look back at my T-Chart. (Point to the T-Chart.) I circled Sleep In Late — that's the side with the most details, the most proof. That's my strongest side. That's what my opinion sentence will be about.

STEP 2. Name the bigger topic. The full prompt that started all this was: "Would you rather stay up late or sleep in late?" I need to choose 1-3 words to include in the opening sentence. I could mention the other side: "stay up late." I might also play around with "rather." That's 4 words, but it would provide the reader with a better idea of why I'm all of a sudden declaring that I like to sleep in late.

STEP 3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Now I need to pick some opinion words. Let's try: should, clearly, best. I'll test these all out to see which one sounds the best.

STEP 4. Put the 3 parts together. Now I put the 3 pieces of information together — 1 of the opinion phrases plus the strongest side ("sleep in late") plus "rather, stay up late." I'll start with "should."
• "You should sleep in late, rather than stay up late." (Pause.) I've got the 3 pieces, but it sounds a little awkward bossy. It doesn't sound persuasive; it sounds demanding. Plus, I don't love using "you." Let me try a different opinion word — clearly.
• "Sleeping in late is clearly better than staying up late." (Pause.) I definitely like the word "clearly." It sounds very strong and authoritative. Let me dabble with "best" in a third attempt.
• "The best is sleeping in late, rather than staying up late." Huh, I don't like that one. It's very wordy. I'm definitely liking the second one I created.

STEP 5. Write the sentence. (Write slowly while narrating: Sleeping… in… late… is… clearly… better… than… staying… up… late.)

Today, we are learning how to write the opening opinion statement — the first sentence of any persuasive piece. Strong persuasive writing begins with a clear, confident opinion statement that the rest of the writing will prove.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another one.
1. Determine the strongest side. Yesterday, we determined that the best pet was a Dog over a Cat.

2. Name the bigger topic. What 3 words from that full prompt do you think should be included? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard several of you mention "pet."

3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Look at the list of opinion words. Identify 3 you would like to play around with. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard several possibilities. Let's go with "best, better, & most."

4. Put the 3 parts together. Let's start with "best." Put that with "dog" and "pet." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "A dog is the best pet." I also heard a couple of you say… "A dog is the best pet anyone can have." Which do you think is stronger? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you note that the longer sentence sounded more persuasive. OK, let's try an opinion sentence with "better." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "Dogs make better pets than cats." Well it's definitely clear. But I'm thinking it sounds more like a compare-contrast and not persuasive enough. Let's try a third option using "most." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "Dogs are the most fun pet." Most fun — how does that sound? And do you prefer the first sentence or this third option? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me.

Today, we are learning how to use opinion words and our strongest side from the T-Chart to write the first sentence of our persuasive piece.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
During Independent Writing Time, you will get out your T-Chart on the best recess equipment — monkey bars or swings. I want you to follow the same process that I just taught you: 1. Name the strongest side. 2. Name the bigger topic. 3. Choose 3 opinion words. 4. Put the parts together. 5. I want you to write 3 opinion sentences — each one using a different opinion word with the strongest side. Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #1: Recognize opinion topics — Grade 4

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that informative writing teaches facts and narrative writing shares stories. But there is a third kind of writing — persuasive writing — where the writer shares what he thinks or believes about a topic. Today, I'm going to teach you how to recognize if a writer/author is sharing an opinion — or not.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing starts with an opinion. An opinion tells what the writer thinks, feels, or believes about a topic that has different sides or choices. Unlike facts — which are right or wrong — opinions are neither. They are simply different. Two people can read about the same topic and believe completely different things. (Introduce the icons & hand gestures.)

When a reader recognizes that a piece of writing is persuasive, he understands: the writer is going to share what HE thinks and explain why his choice is best.

WHY the skill is important | If a reader cannot tell the difference between opinions and facts, he may confuse what the writer believes with fact. This gets trickier in fourth grade — because persuasive writing actually includes facts, details, and real examples. The writer uses those facts to support his opinion. That means a persuasive piece can sound a lot like an informative piece. When readers recognize persuasive writing, they understand: "This is what the author believes — and he is using facts to convince me." Then they can read and decide whether or not to agree.

HOW the skill works | After reading a little bit of the text…
1. ASK: Is the author describing what happened to characters? If yes, then it's a narrative story.
2. ASK: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? If yes — it's informative writing. But remember — persuasive writing also includes facts. So if you see facts, don't stop there. Keep questioning the author's purpose.
3. ASK: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings AND occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (The facts are there to support the opinion, not replace it.) Also look for subtle opinion words & adjectives — words like "should/not, most, best, important, better, necessary." Could someone have a different opinion on this same topic? If yes — it's persuasive writing.

This is how readers determine whether the writer's purpose is to describe a narrative story, inform with facts, or persuade the audience with his opinion.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I figure out what type of writing this is. Project P.E. Text A and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a main character. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "Stretching increases flexibility and reduces the risk of injury." That's a fact — everyone agrees on that. "Muscles that are warmed up can move more easily." True — that's how the body works. (Pause.) Everything here sounds like facts everyone agrees on. But persuasive includes facts, too. So I'm going to double check by asking another set of questions.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings & occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (Scan slowly, pointing to each sentence.) "Taking time to stretch is an important part of any physical activity." Important — could that be an opinion word? (Pause.) Let me think. Would everyone agree that stretching is important? Actually — yes. This is widely accepted. It's not really a debatable side. (Pause.) And I don't see the facts here working to convince me of a position. They are simply explaining how stretching works. (Shake head.) This is informative writing.

OK, I'm going to do this again. I'm going to determine the author's purpose for writing. Project P.E. Text B and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a character or a problem. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to the first sentence.) "Daily movement helps build strength and endurance." That sounds like a fact. "Physical activity supports better concentration in the classroom." That could be true. (Pause.) But just seeing facts doesn't mean this is automatically informative. I know persuasive writing uses facts, too. Let me think about this through the persuasive lens.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings & occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (Point to the first sentence.) "Having P.E. every day would improve student health and focus." Improve — opinion word. Would everyone agree? Some might argue daily P.E. takes too much time away from academics. (Point to the last sentence.) "Daily P.E. would benefit both learning and overall well-being." Benefit — another opinion word. Not everyone agrees on what benefits students most. (Pause.) Ahh, I'm noticing how the facts are working to convince me that daily P.E. is a good idea. It's persuasive!

Today, we are learning how to recognize the signals that indicate an author is sharing his opinion within persuasive writing.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. Project Fire Drill Text A. Read it aloud quickly. Do not ask students to comment.

1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say no — there's no character and nothing is happening to anyone. Let's keep going.

2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? Point to "Repeated practice builds confidence and reduces confusion." and "Students learn exactly where to go and what to do." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say those sound like facts — and they do. But persuasive includes some facts. Let's keep asking.

3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings supported by facts? Point to "Regular fire drills are an essential part of school safety." Is "essential" a fact or opinion word? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Ooh… this is a tough one. "Could someone argue that other safety measures are MORE important?" (Nod.) What about "builds confidence," "reduces confusion," "prevent panic" — are those facts to teach us or convince us? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Right — this is persuasive!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to tell when a writer is sharing his opinion — or not. If we can recognize opinions, then we are closer to being able to write them.

During Independent Writing Time, your job is to read several short texts and apply the same process. You will mark the text with a "P" if you determine it's persuasive and shares an opinion. Mark an "I" if it's informative and teaches facts. Mark an "E" if it's an entertaining narrative story. Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (1 of 2) — Grade 4

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that persuasive writing isn't just about what you think — it's about what you can prove. But how do you know which side you can prove best before you start writing? Today, I'm going to teach you how to think through both sides of a topic to determine the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing is more than just your opinion — it's the strongest opinion you can prove. Writers don't pick a side right away and start writing. Instead, they determine the strongest side by carefully thinking through both choices before committing to one. The strongest side isn't necessarily the one you like best — it's the one you can best prove.

WHY the skill is important | If a writer picks a side too quickly — based only on gut feeling — he may choose the harder side to prove. And "harder to prove" means exactly that: when he sits down to write, he can't think of what to say. Thinking through both sides first helps you find the one that you have the most to say about. And in persuasive writing, it's all about convincing the reader, and you need A LOT of details to make your point.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Look at the persuasive topic and identify both choices. Don't lean either direction yet — just name them side by side and treat them equally.

Step 2: Zip it. Before thinking begins, run your finger across your lips — zip them shut. (Demonstrate the zipper gesture.) Your opinion is locked inside. It's not gone — it's just waiting. You are not allowed to unzip until you have thought carefully through BOTH sides. This is how writers avoid rushing to a decision.

STEP 3: Think like one side. (Reveal the blue hat.) Writers put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. Think like someone who genuinely loves this choice — even if you don't. (Teach students to use their hands and mime placing a hat on their heads.)

To generate strong details, try these strategies.
• Picture someone you know who would love this choice. What would they say is great about it?
• Think small — don't just say "it's fun" or "it's good." Ask yourself: what exactly happens? What does it look, feel, smell, taste, or sound like? Small specific details are always stronger than big general ones.
• Think about what you've seen or heard — a commercial, a conversation, something a friend or family member said. That counts as thinking.

When you've thought of everything you can for that side, take the hat off. (Introduce the gesture of picking up a hat, putting it on, thinking, taking it off, then switching to the other hat.)

STEP 4: Think like the other side. (Take off the blue hat and put on the red one.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice — even if it's not your favorite. Use the same three strategies. Give this side the same honest effort you gave the first one. Your zipper stays shut until you've done both.

This is how writers determine the strongest side — by thinking through both before choosing.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I do this.

Step 1: Name both sides. My topic is: What is better — drive-thru or ordering and eating inside? (Display the choices within a T-Chart.) Those are my two choices. I'm not picking — just naming them.

Step 2: Zip it. My first thought is already in my head. (Run finger across lips — zip.) Locked. Not saying it yet. I have to think through both sides first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I'm putting on the Drive-Thru thinking cap. Let me think like someone who really loves the drive-thru.

OK — think small. What actually happens at a drive-thru? You never even get out of the car. If it's raining or freezing outside — you don't care. You just roll down the window. Little kids stay buckled in their car seats — no unbuckling, no carrying, no chaos. And here's a detail I heard someone say once: you can go through the drive-thru in your pajamas and nobody knows. (Laugh to yourself.) What else? You grab your food and you're gone. No parking spot, no walking across a lot, no waiting for a table. If you're on a road trip, a drive-thru stop is fast — you barely lose any time. Once I started thinking small, the details just kept coming. (Take the hat off.) I'm done thinking like a drive-thru person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Hold up the red hat but don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves eating inside. Honestly, I'm usually in a hurry — drive-thru is fine with me. But I have to zip it and borrow someone else's brain. (Put on the red hat.)

Let me picture someone who loves sitting down inside a restaurant. They walk in, find a table, stretch their legs after a long car ride — that actually feels good after being cramped. They can see the menu up close and take their time choosing. They get free refills. Extra ketchup. Extra napkins — right there at the table.

Think small — what else actually happens? You can go wash your hands before you eat. You can get up and use the bathroom. You sit and talk and laugh with whomever you're with — you're not balancing food on your lap or trying to eat while someone's driving. (Pause.) And what have I heard people say? I've heard parents say eating inside feels like an actual meal — not just grabbing food and rushing off somewhere.

Today, we are learning how to push ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides — even the side we don't know well or wouldn't normally choose.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example.
1. Name both sides. The topic is: Which is the best treat — candy bar or ice cream?
2. Zip it. Locked. Think first.
3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Candy Bar thinking cap. Don't just say "candy bars taste good." Think small! Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard the smell of chocolate when you unwrap it, the gooey caramel stretching when you take a bite, breaking off a piece to share, etc. (Hat off — students mime.)
4. Think like the other side. (Red hat on — students mime.) Now think like an ice cream lover — even if that's not your first choice. Think small. Picture someone standing at the counter choosing flavors. What exactly makes them love it? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard licking the cone before it melts, stacking two flavors, cold and creamy on your tongue, trying a new flavor every time. See how thinking small makes even the unexpected side feel full of details?

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — pushing ourselves to think small and find specific details, even for the side we wouldn't naturally choose.

During Independent Writing Time, you and your partner will think through both sides of this topic: Which is the best vacation — winter break or summer break? When I project the topic, work with your partner to think of every small, specific detail you can for one side. Then switch hats and do the same for the other side. How many details can you two come up with? Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (2 of 2) — Grade 4

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Yesterday we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — putting on each thinking cap and pushing ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides. Today I'm going to teach you how to jot down the details you think of for each side. This will bring us one step closer to determining the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Yesterday you thought through both sides of a persuasive topic. But thinking alone isn't enough — ideas that stay in your head slip away before they ever make it into writing. Jotting captures each detail on paper during prewriting. Jotting means writing a concise phrase — 1-4 words to preserve the thinking without slowing down the process. (Connect to research unit jotting if previously taught — Skill 1, Day 2. Review shortcuts and abbreviations.)

WHY the skill is important | A persuasive writer's goal isn't just to list details — it's to jot as many details for BOTH sides as he can think of during prewriting. This is critical to determining the strongest side.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Write one choice at the top of each side of the T-Chart — blue hat side on the left, red hat side on the right. Both sides start equal.

Step 2: Zip it. (Zipper gesture — students mime.) Lock in your first instinct. Don't let it out yet. A writer who commits too early may miss the stronger argument entirely.

STEP 3: Think like one side & jot. (Reveal the blue hat. Students mime.) Put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. Jot each detail in 1–4 words, on its own line, & stacking it down that side. Writers typically begin with one side and continue until ideas slow.

If you fill every line on that side before you're finished thinking — grab a second T-Chart and continue on the same side. The other side stays empty for now. Stay in that thinking cap until every detail is captured. (Remove blue hat. Students mime.)

STEP 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat. Students mime.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice. Jot each detail on its own line, stacking down that side. Give this side the same honest effort.

Writers typically begin with one side and continue until ideas slow down. However, sometimes while making the second list (Side B), the writer has a new thought for Side A. No problem. Jump over to Side A and jot it. Then return to Side B and continue listing details.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I jot details for both sides of my persuasive topic.

Step 1: Name both sides. Yesterday my topic was: What is better — drive-thru or ordering and eating inside? (Display a blank T-Chart.) I write one choice at the top of each side. (Write Drive-thru on the left & Order/Eat In on the right.) There — both sides are named.

Step 2: Zip it. (Run finger across lips — zip.)

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I've got my Drive Thru thinking cap on. Yesterday I thought of several details for this side. Now I jot them — 1–4 words each, stacking down the left side.

(Jot while narrating details.)
• Never get out — car
• Rain/cold — don't care
• Kids stay buckled
• PJs — nobody knows
• Grab food & go
• No parking, no walking
• Road trip — barely lose time

Once I started jotting, the details stacked up fast. (Take the hat off.) I think I'm done thinking like a Drive Thru person.

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Hold up the red hat — don't put it on yet.) Now I have to like someone who loves eating inside. I'm usually in a hurry — drive-thru is fine with me. But I have to zip it and borrow someone else's brain. (Put on the red hat.) Any details I come up with now, will all go on the right side — under "Order & Eat Inside." (Point at T-Chart.)

• I'm picturing someone walking in, finding a table, stretching their legs. (Jot: "stretch legs.")
• See menu up close — take time choosing. (Jot: "see menu, choose.")
• Free refills. (Jot: "free refills.")
• Wash hands before eating. (Jot: "wash hands.")
• Extra ketchup, extra napkins. (Jot: "extra ketchup/napkins.")

(Pause.) Wait — I just thought of something for the Drive-Thru side. (Switch hats.) When you do a lot of drive-thrus, you have a whole pile of extra napkins in the glove compartment. This is valuable! I have to jump back to Side A and capture that before I lose it. (Jot: "extra napkins.")

OK — back to eating inside. (Switch hats back.)
• Sit, talk & laugh with whoever you're with. (Jot: "sit, talk & laugh.")
• Feels like an actual meal — not rushing. (Jot: "actual meal, no rush.")

Today, we are learning how to jot details for both sides of a persuasive topic — capturing specific details on paper so we can eventually determine the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Yesterday, you thought about which is the better treat — a candy bar or ice cream? Help me jot down those details. (Reveal a new T-Chart.)

1. Name both sides. Point in the air — where do I write down the two sides, the two choices? Yes, Candy bar by the blue hat & Ice cream by the red hat.

2. Zip it. Locked. Think first.

3. Think like one side & jot. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — "smell choc, melt in mouth, gooey & stretchy caramel, easy to share = break," etc.

4. Think like the other side & jot. (Switch hats.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — licking, stack scoops & flavors, creamy, try new flavors, cold on tongue, etc. Does any of this make you think of another detail about Candy bar? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard some of you say that chocolate is thick & creamy, too. (Switch hats & jot it.)

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think & jot down details for BOTH sides of a persuasive. This is an important step before we can determine the strongest side.

During Independent Writing Time, you will fill out a T-Chart for which is the best vacation — winter break or summer break. This time you will work alone. (Yesterday you brainstormed with a partner. Today, you will jot down the details by yourself.) Think of all the details you can for one side before switching to the other side. And if you need a second T-Chart, I've got extra ones right here. Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #3: Write an opinion — Grade 4

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Up until now, everything we have done in our persuasive unit has been prewriting — thinking through both sides and determining the strongest one. Today we transition from prewriting to drafting. The first thing a persuasive writer does in his draft is tell the audience which side he has chosen. Today, I'm going to teach you how to write a strong opinion statement at the beginning of any persuasive piece.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing begins with an opinion statement. The first sentence tells the audience exactly what the writer thinks and which side he has chosen. This is no longer prewriting — this is the moment the writer goes public with his thinking.

WHY the skill is important | Without a clear opinion statement at the opening, the reader has no anchor — he doesn't know what side the writer is on or what the writing is trying to prove. By stating the opinion first, the writer signals his position immediately and sets up everything that follows. Remember — the goal of persuasive writing is to convince the audience to agree. So get to the point fast.

HOW the skill works |
STEP 1. Name the strongest side. Look back at your T-Chart. Find the side circled — the one with the most details and proof. The word or words labeling that side belong in your opinion sentence.

STEP 2. Name the bigger topic. This is typically found in the writing prompt. It's the broader subject the two sides come from — usually 1–3 words. It gives the reader context so the opinion doesn't appear out of nowhere.

STEP 3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. (Connect to SKILL #1 — opinion signal words.) By intermediate grades, writers rarely use "I think" or "I believe" in persuasive writing. Opinion language is much more subtle. It's drops a single word — like "should, clearly, or best" — rather than a sentence starter. Test out 3 different opinion words as options for the first sentence.

STEP 4. Put the 3 parts together. Combine all 3 items in one oral sentence: strongest side + bigger topic + opinion word. Try it different ways, each time using different opinion language. Listen for the version that is most direct, most confident, and most specific. The stronger and more precise that opening statement, the more confident and convincing the entire piece feels from the first sentence forward.

STEP 5. Write the sentence. The one that sounds the best is the sentence to write. This is how all persuasive writing should begin — with a clear, confident opinion statement that the rest of the writing will prove.

(NOTE: Stop there. The first sentence only names the opinion. No details. No "because." See SKILL #5 for where the "because" fits in persuasive writing.)

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I do this.

Step 1: Name the strongest side. I look back at my T-Chart. (Point to the T-Chart.) I circled Drive thru — that's the side with the most details, the most proof. That's my strongest side. That's what my opinion sentence will be about.

STEP 2. Name the bigger topic. The full prompt that started all this was: "Which is better when ordering and eating food from a restaurant: drive thru or going inside?" I need to choose 1-3 words to include in the opening sentence. Well I definitely can't just say "drive thru." That's totally out of the blue. I need to reference "ordering & eating food."

STEP 3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Now I need to pick some opinion words. Let's try: clearly, definitely, & no doubt. I'll test these all to see which one sounds the best.

STEP 4. Put the 3 parts together. Now I put the 3 pieces of information together — 1 of the opinion phrases plus the strongest side ("drive thru") plus "ordering & eating food." I'll start with "clearly."
• "When ordering and eating food from a restaurant, the drive-thru is clearly the better choice." (Pause.) I like "clearly" — it sounds confident and authoritative. I also worked in "better" as a second opinion word. Let me try "definitely."
• "The drive-thru is definitely the way to order & eat food from a restaurant." (Pause.) I like the power of "definitely" but without mentioning the other side, it sounds awkward to be so positive about something. Let me try "no doubt" in a third attempt.
• "There is no doubt that ordering & eating from the drive-thru is better than eating inside." (Pause.) Oooh, I like that. It's a little long, but it sets up the context for my reader. I think it's the best option.

STEP 5. Write the sentence. (Write it slowly while narrating.)

Today, we are learning how to write the opening opinion statement — the first sentence of any persuasive piece. Strong persuasive writing begins with a clear, confident opinion statement that the rest of the writing will prove.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another one.
1. Determine the strongest side. Yesterday, we determined that the best treat was a Candy bar over ice cream.

2. Name the bigger topic. What 3 words from that full prompt do you think should be included? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard several of you mention "best treat."

3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Look at the list of opinion words. Identify 3 you would like to play around with. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard several possibilities. Let's go with "only, clearly, & should."

4. Put the 3 parts together. Let's start with "only." Put that with "candy bar" and "treat" or "best treat." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "I think a candy bar is clearly the best treat." What is strong and not-so-strong in this opinion statement? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you note that we don't want to start with "I think…" anymore. That worked in first grade, but not in fourth! OK, let's try an opinion sentence with "clearly." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "A candy bar is clearly the only treat you should ever pick." Well it's definitely better than the first one. How do you feel about "clearly?" How would the reader take that? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. Let's try a third option using "should." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "Everyone should choose a candy bar because it is the best treat." Do you like this one better than the second one — why? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me.

Today, we are learning how to use opinion words and our strongest side from the T-Chart to write the first sentence of our persuasive piece.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
During Independent Writing Time, you will get out your T-Chart on what is better — Winter break or Summer break? I want you to follow the same process that I just taught you: 1. Name the strongest side. 2. Name the bigger topic. 3. Choose 3 opinion words. 4. Put the parts together. 5. I want you to write 3 opinion sentences — each one using a different opinion word with the strongest side. Now it's your turn!
